verdict.summary: In fp48_write_bin's packed branch, the compressed element computed by fp48_pck(t, a) is never used: all four output writes serialize the raw, unnormalized coefficients of the input 'a' (a[0][1], a[0][2], a[1][0], a[1][2]) while discarding a[0][0]/a[1][1] without normalization. With pack=1 and len == 32*RLC_FP_BYTES the length check passes, the function completes successfully, and bin receives a 32-byte 'packed' encoding that does not represent the packed form of the element — silently incorrect serialization of cryptographic state presented as a valid packed encoding; deserializing it reconstructs a value different from the one serialized.

evidence.reason: fp48_pck(t, a) computes the packed (normalized, compressed) element into t, but every subsequent write serializes the raw coefficients of the input a instead of t; t is never read on any path. Since the packed 32-byte format stores only 4 of the 6 fp8 coefficients and drops a[0][0] and a[1][1], the packing step is what makes those dropped coefficients recoverable; serializing a's unnormalized coefficients makes the output an incorrect, non-canonical 'packed' encoding. Trigger fully instantiated: call with pack=1, len == 32*RLC_FP_BYTES (quoted check at lines 10-12 passes), any valid fp48 element — the function returns success having written bytes that do not represent the packed form of the element.

evidence.snippet: fp48_new(t);
evidence.reason: Origin of the discarded packed value: t is allocated solely to hold the result of fp48_pck(t, a) at line 13, yet is never used by any statement in the function — structural proof that the packed-branch writes at lines 14-17 were intended to consume t and instead consume the raw input a.

assumptions: fp48_pck(t, a) transforms/normalizes its input (callee not shown); this is inferred from necessity: the packed 32-byte format discards a[0][0] and a[1][1], which are unrecoverable from the stored four coefficients unless the element was first normalized — the sole purpose of the fp48_pck call and of allocating t.
RLC_FP_BYTES is a small compile-time constant, so 32*RLC_FP_BYTES and 48*RLC_FP_BYTES cannot overflow int.
The listing appears truncated: RLC_TRY closes at line 25 with no RLC_CATCH_ANY/RLC_FINALLY block and no closing brace, so the standard fp48_free(t) cleanup cannot be assessed.
limitations: bin == NULL with a correct len would be dereferenced by fp8_write_bin at line 14 (no NULL guard exists in the given code, CWE-476), but the trigger requires the same-process caller to pass NULL; no cross-trust-boundary party is exhibitable in this code, so it is not counted as a finding.
Possible leak of t (fp48_new at line 7 with no fp48_free in the shown lines) is attributable to the truncated listing, not to a demonstrable defect.

Concrete downstream harm of the wrong packed encoding (e.g., failed pairing verification or encoding malleability when fp48_read_bin(pack=1) decompresses the wrong bytes) occurs in consumer code not given; the in-code impact is the silent emission of a misrepresentative packed serialization under a success path.

verdict.summary: display_dollar() forms the pointer p + col from the caller-supplied column and the current line text without any bound of col against the line length, and passes it to mb_head_off which inspects that byte. When col exceeds the length of the (untrusted, file-derived) current line, p + col points past the line buffer's NUL terminator, producing an out-of-bounds heap read at an attacker-influenced offset. No bounds, clamp, or range check on col exists anywhere in the function.

evidence.snippet:
p = ml_get_curline();
	curwin->w_cursor.col -= (*mb_head_off)(p, p + col);
evidence.reason: Root cause: out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) caused by unvalidated index handling (CWE-129). p is the untrusted current-line text (line 16) and col is an unvalidated column parameter; the pointer p + col is formed and passed to mb_head_off with no statement bounding col to the line length. Instantiated trigger: caller supplies col = 40 while the line is "ab" (file content); p + 40 lies 37 bytes past the NUL of a 3-byte buffer, and mb_head_off reads the byte at that address — an out-of-bounds heap read reachable across the file-content/caller trust boundary.

evidence.snippet:
display_dollar(colnr_T col)
{
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: col enters as the parameter of this non-static, exported function. No documented precondition, assert, or bounds check on col is present anywhere in the given code, so col is attacker-data; the caller's supposed validation is not quotable and cannot dismiss the defect.

assumptions: mb_head_off is assumed to dereference its second argument (the comment 'If on the last byte of a multi-byte move to the first byte' describes that purpose); its implementation is not shown.
ml_get_curline() is assumed to return a NUL-terminated buffer whose extent ends at the line's NUL; its implementation is not shown.
The width of colnr_T (int in the surrounding codebase) is not quotable from the given code; the defect is width-independent because col can exceed the line length at any practical width.
limitations: The subsequent call curs_columns(FALSE) with a possibly mis-adjusted curwin->w_cursor.col may read further out of bounds, but that use occurs inside a callee not shown; its impact is not instantiated in this code.

A signed underflow of curwin->w_cursor.col at line 17 (if mb_head_off returned more than col) is only reachable once p + col is already out of bounds; it is a derivative of the confirmed OOB read, not an independent finding.
edit_putchar and the w_wcol < w_width check (line 20) were examined and found properly ordered and unrelated to the defect; no additional findings there.

verdict.summary: The function consumes an attacker-controlled endpoint name and passes it to strncpy/connect without a length or NUL-termination check, but the copy is bounded by the exact destination array size, so no out-of-bounds access occurs in this code; every remaining candidate's security impact either executes in code not given (kernel handling of an unterminated/truncated AF_UNIX path, caller-side effects of connecting to a truncated prefix) or requires a trigger precondition (fd >= FD_SETSIZE at FD_SET; select() failure plus SO_ERROR==0 while still in progress) that the given statements cannot instantiate. All error paths were verified fail-closed: sockFd is set to -1 on every failure branch and addToActiveSockets is guarded by 'if (sockFd >= 0)'.

assumptions: FATAL_FAIL(x) aborts or otherwise handles negative/failing values; its definition is not given.
initSocket(sockFd) sets the socket non-blocking; only implied by the EINPROGRESS handling, not shown.
sockaddr_un layout with sizeof == 110 and sun_path == 108 bytes (typical Linux) is assumed; the code uses sizeof(remote.sun_path) directly.
The implementations of endpoint.name(), operator<<(endpoint), GetErrno/SetErrno, and addToActiveSockets are not shown; none is relied on to demote a candidate.
Deployment context (daemon/library, privilege level, who calls connect and how often) is not quotable and was not used to judge any candidate.
limitations: strncpy(remote.sun_path, pipePath.c_str(), sizeof(remote.sun_path)) does not guarantee NUL termination and silently truncates names of length >= sizeof(sun_path) (CWE-170 class). Trigger is fully instantiated (a >=108-char endpoint.name() reaches this line unvalidated — no length check exists anywhere in the function), but the security consequence lives outside this code: the unterminated 108-byte attacker-chosen path is consumed by kernel pathname resolution (not given), and since the name is attacker-data per STEP 1, connecting to a truncated attacker-chosen prefix grants no capability this code's contract doesn't already grant. A caller intending a longer trusted path would connect elsewhere, but that caller and its reliance are not shown.

FD_SET(sockFd, &fdset) / select(sockFd + 1, ...) perform an out-of-bounds bit write into the 128-byte fd_set on the stack when sockFd >= FD_SETSIZE (CWE-787 class, memory corruption). No upper-bound check exists anywhere in the function, but instantiating the trigger requires the process to hold >=1023 open descriptors with a raised RLIMIT_NOFILE at the moment socket() returns; no statement in this code (nor any quotable caller loop) produces that state, so the trigger is speculative.

The return value of select() is ignored; if select fails (e.g., EINTR), FD_ISSET may read a stale set and ::getsockopt(SO_ERROR) returning 0 while the non-blocking connect is still pending would take the 'Connected to endpoint' branch, presenting an unverified connection as connected. The trigger requires an OS/signal-induced select failure and getsockopt semantics that are not quotable from the given code.
LOG(INFO) << sockFd << " is a good socket" prints '-1 is a good socket' on failure paths; cosmetic only, since the returned value and addToActiveSockets are correctly guarded by 'if (sockFd >= 0)'.

verdict.summary: validate_event() guards the indirect call armpmu->get_event_idx() only by comparing event->pmu with event->group_leader->pmu (and two state checks). A perf event on a non-ARM (software) PMU that leads its own group (group_leader == event, so leader_pmu == event->pmu, and state INACTIVE or OFF with user-set enable_on_exec) passes both guards, so to_arm_pmu(event->pmu) fabricates a struct arm_pmu pointer from the software PMU object and the code calls a get_event_idx function pointer loaded from memory outside any arm_pmu object. The path is reachable via perf_event_open() mixed hardware/software groups (user-chosen group composition and user-controlled attr.enable_on_exec), yielding a wild kernel function-pointer call from an unprivileged syscall: a control-flow corruption primitive / out-of-bounds read, and at minimum a kernel oops (DoS).

evidence.reason: The sink at line 13, `armpmu->get_event_idx(hw_events, event)`, requires that `armpmu` (line 4, `to_arm_pmu(event->pmu)`) point to a real arm_pmu with a valid get_event_idx. The only pmu-related guard (lines 7-8) compares `event->pmu` to `event->group_leader->pmu` — it does not verify that event->pmu is the ARM PMU. Instantiated trigger: a software event S leading its own group (S->group_leader == S, so leader_pmu == S->pmu == &software_pmu, state INACTIVE) passes both checks (the state guard at lines 10-11 also fails open at the OFF boundary when the user sets attr.enable_on_exec), so line 13 calls a function pointer loaded from offsetof(struct arm_pmu, get_event_idx) computed off the software PMU object — an out-of-object read and wild indirect call in kernel context, reachable via perf_event_open group composition.

assumptions: The caller (group-validation path) is not shown; per the methodology its parameters are treated as attacker-data carrying user-controlled perf_event content (group composition via group_fd, attr.enable_on_exec), and 'the caller only passes ARM-PMU events' is an unquotable contract that may not demote the finding.
to_arm_pmu() is assumed to be a container_of-style cast with no type validation; it is not shown in the given code.
PERF_EVENT_STATE_OFF = -1 and INACTIVE = 0 (standard perf enum values) are assumed for the boundary analysis of the state checks at lines 7 and 10.
limitations: NULL-pointer dereference of `event->group_leader` at line 5: the trigger precondition (a perf_event with group_leader == NULL) cannot be instantiated from any statement in this code, and perf core always initializes group_leader (contract outside the given code) — speculative, not counted as a finding.

The exact value loaded as the get_event_idx function pointer (and thus crash-vs-hijack) depends on kernel memory layout adjacent to the software PMU structs, which is outside the given code; the security-relevant fact is the out-of-object load and unconditional indirect call itself.

verdict.summary: This init function allocates two resources and checks both failure sentinels in execution order (`if (!s->frame) return AVERROR(ENOMEM);` and `if (!s->vert_pred) { av_frame_free(&s->frame); return AVERROR(ENOMEM); }`), with no leak, double free, uninitialized use, or attacker-reachable corruption within the given statements. The attacker-controlled value avctx->width (container-derived) flows only into an allocation-size expression; on the types the code uses (size_t arithmetic) no wrap occurs for any int width — extreme values yield allocation failure caught by the quoted NULL checks and a clean ENOMEM return. The only residual hazard — an undersized vert_pred from a 32-bit size_t wrap, or a later width change before decode — has its harmful use entirely in the decode function, which is not part of the given code, so the impact chain cannot be instantiated here.

assumptions: avctx and avctx->priv_data are assumed non-NULL by the FFmpeg framework; no statement in the given code documents or asserts this contract, so NULL-dereference resistance is an assumption, not a verified guard.
av_frame_alloc and av_fast_malloc are assumed to return NULL / leave the pointer NULL exactly on allocation failure (standard failure-sentinel behavior); their implementations are not shown.
size_t is assumed to be at least 64 bits on the target for the width*4 expression; the code itself only fixes sizeof(unsigned int)=4 and relies on size_t promotion.
limitations: avctx->width is attacker-controlled (container/demuxer data) and is used to size s->vert_pred (width * sizeof(unsigned int)). If width could change between init and decode, or if the decode function (not given) indexes vert_pred by a per-frame dimension larger than the init-time width, an out-of-bounds access would occur there — that use is outside the given code, so no vulnerability can be confirmed here.

On a target where size_t is 32 bits, width = 2^30 + 1 makes width*4 wrap to 4, producing a 4-byte vert_pred where ~4 GiB would be needed; the undersized buffer is only harmful in the not-shown decode function, and the wrap requires 32-bit size_t behavior while the code's expression types are wider (size_t) on the canonical target — speculative.
No path in this code writes to or indexes vert_pred; consequently even a mis-sized allocation causes no memory-safety violation within the given statements.

verdict.summary: get_netloc treats everything after '://' up to the first '/' as the netloc, including URL query ('?') and fragment ('#') components. The subdomain check in get_target_for_redirect therefore only verifies that this mixed string ends with '.' + domain, so a target such as 'https://evil.com?.example.com' passes the check (netloc = 'evil.com?.example.com' ends with '.example.com') while its real host is attacker-controlled. The function then returns the raw attacker URL as the validated in-domain redirect target, fully bypassing the domain allowlist (open redirect).

evidence.reason: Root cause (sink): this suffix test compares a string that is not guaranteed to be the host. With target = 'https://evil.com?.example.com' and domain = 'example.com', target_netloc = 'evil.com?.example.com' (size 21): size 21 > 11 passes, compare(10, 11, 'example.com') == 0 passes, target_netloc[9] == '.' passes, so the raw attacker-controlled URL is assigned to result and returned as the in-domain redirect target even though its actual host is evil.com.

Origin of the tainted value: the extraction loop's only terminator is '/' (url[start] != '/'), so query ('?') and fragment ('#') characters and everything after them are copied into netloc. For 'https://evil.com?.example.com' the loop copies 'evil.com?.example.com' (it never sees a '/'), letting attacker-chosen query text satisfy the domain-suffix check performed by the caller.

assumptions: get_target_for_redirect is the public API that decides the redirect destination; the caller is untrusted for the 'target' parameter, so no caller-side validation of 'target' is assumed.
The only consumer of the returned URL shown in this code is main(), which prints it to stdout; the analysis treats the function itself as the intake point making the in-domain certification decision.
limitations: Scheme is never validated: matched targets are returned verbatim, so 'http://example.com' or 'javascript://example.com/x' are accepted despite the docstring 'Use https protocol' (line 31). The exploitable consequence of a javascript:/http: redirect target exists in the (not shown) consumer, so this is recorded as a secondary weakness rather than a separate primary finding.
Userinfo-based targets such as 'https://example.com@evil.com' are rejected (char before suffix is '@', not '.'), so no bypass was found via '@'.
argv[0] dereference on line 69 could be NULL only if the process were exec'd with an empty argv (argc == 0); this environment-only trigger is speculative and not treated as a finding.

No memory-safety defects: all indexing (line 19 'start < url.size()', line 54 'target_netloc.size() > domain.size()') was verified as guarded on every path, and the compare position is always within bounds.

verdict.summary: The setting-name security check handles attacker-controlled names safely: std::string::compare(0,7,"secure.") cannot throw or over-read for any length including empty and shorter-than-7 names; the log sink is reachable only after an exact-equality guard that restricts the streamed value to the literals "mg_name"/"mg_flags", so no log forging is possible; the only pointer result consumed is nullptr-tested. The residual concern — that "secure.*" settings are blocked only when ScriptApiSecurity::isSecure(L) is true, and that mainmenu code may set mapgen settings — could not be developed into an in-code impact chain, since the effect of such writes is determined by consumers not shown.

assumptions: The caller of checkSettingSecurity is assumed to interpret return value -1 as failure and 0 as success, and to propagate the thrown LuaError; no statement in the given code shows this.

ScriptApiSecurity::isSecure(L) and ModApiBase::getGuiEngine(L) semantics (what a non-secure environment may do, and which environments have a GUI engine) are external to the given code and are treated as assumptions, not evidence.
Setting names are assumed to be stored and looked up as exact strings with no case folding or normalization elsewhere; no statement in this code performs or documents normalization.
script_get_backtrace(L) output is assumed to be engine-generated diagnostic content, not attacker-composed text.
limitations: Candidate dismissed (authz gap, CWE-862-adjacent): the block on "secure."-prefixed settings is gated by 'ScriptApiSecurity::isSecure(L) && name.compare(0, 7, "secure.") == 0', so in a non-secure Lua environment a mod could write secure.* settings (e.g. a name such as "secure.enable_security") without triggering the throw. No unconditional or environment-independent check on any path blocks this. Dismissed because the harm of such a write is instantiated only in setting consumers not given, and a non-secure environment's pre-existing capabilities are not established by any quotable statement here.

Candidate dismissed (by-design branch): when 'ModApiBase::getGuiEngine(L) != nullptr' (mainmenu), the mg_name/mg_flags restriction is skipped by the '!is_mainmenu' condition; the downstream effect of a mainmenu mapgen setting is outside this code.

Candidate tested and refuted (log forging, CWE-117): errorstream write of 'name' is guarded in execution order by 'name == "mg_name" || name == "mg_flags"', so only literal content reaches the log; boundary-tested with empty, 6-char, 7-char, and case-flipped names — compare(0,7,…) neither throws nor misclassifies any of them.

verdict.summary: The directory-containment check `file_realpath_str.find(dir_realpath_str) != 0` is a bare string-prefix test without a trailing path separator. A filename containing '../' that resolves to a sibling entry whose name extends the directory's name (e.g. dir '/data', filename '../data2/secret' resolving to '/data2/secret') passes the check, and the file outside the intended directory is opened and returned — a path-traversal escape of the restricted directory (CWE-22).

evidence.reason: The only containment guard is a string-prefix test with no path-separator boundary: for dir realpath '/data' and file realpath '/data2/secret', find('/data') returns 0 so the guard passes, and the ifstream on line 43 opens the out-of-directory path, returning its contents. Trigger instantiated with filename='../data2/secret', dir_path='/data'.

evidence.snippet: std::string file_path = dir_path + "/" + filename;
evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled filename (no validation of '..', '/', or any component anywhere in the function) is concatenated into the file path that realpath resolves and the ifstream on line 43 opens; this is the taint origin for the traversal that the defective prefix check on line 38 fails to contain.

assumptions: Deployment context (CLI, service, privilege level) is unknown and was not used; argv strings and any caller-supplied arguments to the exported function are treated as attacker-data because no documented/quoted caller precondition exists in the code.

The traversal trigger requires a filesystem sibling entry whose name extends the chosen directory's name (e.g. '/data2' beside '/data'); the attacker also fully controls dir_path, so any directory on the system with such a sibling satisfies the precondition, but the existence of such a sibling is an environment state, not a statement in this code.
limitations: TOCTOU symlink swap between realpath (line 32) and the ifstream open (line 43): the two ordered operations exist in this code, but no statement establishes that an attacker can write into the directory between them, so the race precondition is speculative.

The realpath output buffers are 1024 bytes (lines 21, 31) while POSIX requires a PATH_MAX-sized buffer (4096 on Linux); a resolved path of 1025-4095 bytes would overflow. The out-of-bounds write itself occurs inside libc (not shown) and requires an attacker-constructed deep directory tree, so the impact chain breaks outside this code and this is recorded as a limitation rather than a confirmed finding.

verdict.summary: secure_check is the trust-boundary intake for an untrusted boot image, yet after decrypting the image header in place it validates only the magic field: the attacker-derived header->file_size is passed unvalidated as the processing length to secure_decrypt(file, header->file_size, 1) at line 14. No statement in the function bounds, clamps, or checks file_size against the loaded image size in any form, so an image whose decrypted header carries an oversized file_size drives in-place memory processing (evidenced by the line 6 in-place decrypt followed by reading the header from data at lines 9-10) far past the loaded image buffer, enabling out-of-bounds read/write in the secure-boot path.

evidence.snippet:
file = (unsigned char *)data + sizeof(*header);
	return secure_decrypt(file, header->file_size, 1);
evidence.reason: Sink: the decrypted (attacker-influenced) header field file_size is used directly as the length argument to secure_decrypt operating on file = data + sizeof(*header). The precondition that file_size not exceed the remaining loaded image size is enforced by no statement in this code; STEP 5 searched for a bounds check, clamp, corrected comparison, resized buffer, checked accessor, rejecting error arm, and failure-sentinel test on every path and found none (the only prior validation is the magic comparison, which constrains a different field). Trigger fully instantiated: line 6 decrypts attacker content in place, the magic check passes for a header with matching magic, and any file_size value (including boundary values 0 or the field maximum) flows unguarded into the length-consuming call, causing memory processing beyond the loaded image buffer.

Origin/missing-check site: this is the only validation applied to the decrypted, untrusted header, and it examines only the magic field. Reading header->magic from data itself also evidences that secure_decrypt operates in place (the decrypted bytes reside at data), which is what makes the unbounded file_size at line 14 a memory-corruption-capable length rather than a mere count. A size check on header->file_size belongs immediately after this magic check and is absent.

assumptions: The definitions of at91_secure_header_t, AT91_SECURE_MAGIC, and secure_decrypt are not shown; the width and signedness of header->file_size and the exact signature of secure_decrypt are assumed (typically an unsigned 32-bit size and a size_t length parameter). The analysis does not depend on the width: no guard exists for any value.

The caller supplies a non-NULL data pointer pointing to a buffer of at least sizeof(*header) bytes; this precondition is not documented, asserted, or checked anywhere in the given code, so it is an assumption, not a fact.
That secure_decrypt authenticates or bounds the length internally is an unquotable callee contract and was NOT used to dismiss the finding; per guard anchoring it does not exist for this analysis.
Deployment context (boot ROM, setuid, library) cannot be quoted from the code and was not used to promote or demote any candidate.
limitations: NULL data dereference at line 10 (header->magic): the trigger requires the caller to pass NULL, a state no statement in this code produces and no attacker input channel in this code sets (only the buffer content is attacker-controlled); worst case is a crash. Speculative, not counted.
Pointer wrap of data + sizeof(*header) at line 13 requires data within sizeof(*header) bytes of the address-space top; not producible by any shown statement. Speculative.

The first call secure_decrypt(data, sizeof(*header), 0) uses a fixed compile-time length; if the caller supplies a buffer smaller than the header, the OOB access occurs inside the not-shown callee under a caller contract this code never checks — trigger not instantiated here.

The exact byte-level effect of the unbounded file_size (out-of-bounds read vs. write) occurs inside secure_decrypt, which is not shown; the in-place processing pattern is inferred from this code's own lines 6 and 9-10 rather than quoted from the callee. This does not demote the finding because this code passes the attacker-derived length that the callee consumes and is the intake point that failed to validate it.

verdict.summary: This thin wrapper for PHP compact() guards its only in-code hazard (NULL VarEnv) with 'if (v)' on the sole path to the compact() calls. The sole attacker-influenced computation, 'args.size() + 1' for a reserve hint, can only overflow at SIZE_MAX-scale array sizes that cannot be instantiated, and MakeReserve is an allocation hint on a growable Array, not a memory-safety bound. All variable-name lookups and insertions occur inside the unshown compact() callee, so no defect statement with an instantiated trigger and quoted impact chain exists in this code.

assumptions: __SystemLib_compact_sl is a runtime function reachable with script-controlled values (varname and args content treated as attacker-data); the code itself quotes no caller contract for either parameter.
PackedArray::MakeReserve is treated as a reservation hint for a dynamically growable HHVM Array rather than a fixed buffer bound; this is internal HHVM semantics not quotable from the given code.
getOrCreateVarEnv() is assumed to create a VarEnv when absent, making the NULL path a degenerate internal condition; its behavior is not quotable from the given code.
The unshown compact(VarEnv*, Array&, ...) helper's behavior (name-to-string conversion, VarEnv lookup bounds, ret insertion growth) is unknown.
limitations: Integer overflow of 'args.size() + 1' (CWE-190) could not be instantiated: it requires an Array with SIZE_MAX-scale element count, which no statement in this code or any allocatable process can produce.

Reserve mismatch: ret is reserved for args.size() + 1 while varname may itself be an array of names; if compact() inserted into a fixed-size buffer this would be CWE-131, but the insertion logic is entirely inside the unshown compact() callee and the reserve is a hint, so the impact chain breaks at an unquoted link.
Any bounds, string-conversion, or lookup defects in the compact() helper itself are not analyzable because that function is not part of the given code.
Returning an empty array when the VarEnv is NULL is degenerate data-return, not security-state misrepresentation, since compact() is not an authn/authz/verification primitive.

verdict.summary: In tty_ioctl, the TIOCGETD case dereferences tty->ldisc and tty->ldisc->ops ('return put_user(tty->ldisc->ops->num, (int __user *)p);') without taking a line-discipline reference or lock, while this same handler dispatches TIOCSETD ('return tiocsetd(tty, p);') and TIOCVHANGUP ('tty_vhangup(tty);'), which concurrently replace and free the current ldisc. Two threads racing TIOCGETD against TIOCSETD on the same tty produce a use-after-free read of kernel heap memory (and a stale ops-pointer dereference); every other ldisc access in the function is performed under tty_ldisc_ref_wait/tty_ldisc_deref, proving the required guard exists elsewhere but is absent on this path.

evidence.snippet:
case TIOCGETD:
		return put_user(tty->ldisc->ops->num, (int __user *)p);
evidence.reason: Unguarded two-level dereference of tty->ldisc (and tty->ldisc->ops) with no ldisc reference held: no tty_ldisc_ref_wait/tty_ldisc_deref or lock lies on the TIOCGETD path (the first switch at lines 17-32 does not include TIOCGETD, and the reference taken at line 138 is unreachable because this case returns here). Instantiated trigger: an unprivileged thread issues TIOCGETD on a tty while another thread issues TIOCSETD via this same handler, swapping and freeing the old ldisc between the load of tty->ldisc and the ->ops dereference, yielding a use-after-free read (CWE-416) of kernel heap reachable across the userspace trust boundary.

Origin of the racing mutation: this same ioctl handler dispatches TIOCSETD (requiring no capability beyond tty_check_change at lines 23-24) and TIOCVHANGUP, both of which replace tty->ldisc and drop the reference on the previous line discipline. Nothing in the given code serializes these statements with the unprotected tty->ldisc dereference at line 73, so the race window is two ordered operations in this code with attacker-controlled interleaving.

Counterfactual-guard contrast: the function's own ldisc-ioctl tail takes a reference ('ld = tty_ldisc_ref_wait(tty);') before touching ld->ops and releases it ('tty_ldisc_deref(ld);'), demonstrating that ldisc access requires a reference — a guard that is present on this fall-through path but absent on the TIOCGETD path at line 73, confirming the STEP 5 fix-form search (no reference, lock, NULL check, checked accessor, or rejecting error arm exists between line 72 and the sink).

assumptions: tiocsetd (TIOCSETD) and tty_vhangup (TIOCVHANGUP) replace tty->ldisc and drop the last reference on the previous line discipline, freeing it — standard kernel callee behavior, not quotable from the given code.
put_user/copy primitives are fault-safe against attacker-supplied user pointers; tty_paranoia_check validates the tty pointer itself (line 9).
tty_ldisc_ref_wait/tty_ldisc_deref acquire and release a line-discipline reference (inferred from their names and usage pattern; bodies not shown).
limitations: TIOCSTI is dispatched here ('return tiocsti(tty, p);', line 39) and is a known terminal-input-injection vector, but its permission check and handling are entirely inside tiocsti, which is not shown; the impact chain cannot be instantiated in the given code.

verdict.summary: In keyfetch_done(), the return value of dns_rdata_fromstruct() is discarded at all three call sites while marshalling attacker-derived KEYDATA into the fixed 4096-byte stack buffer key_buf. A DNSKEY RRset fetched from the remotely managed zone (the RFC5011 adversary this code exists to defend against) can contain a KSK-flagged key whose marshalled KEYDATA exceeds 4096 bytes, so the conversion fails (buffer bounded by isc_buffer_init(&keyb, key_buf, sizeof(key_buf))), yet the resulting invalid keydatarr is passed unchecked to update_one_rr() and committed into the managed-keys trust-anchor database via zone_journal(). Every other parse in this function is checked (RUNTIME_CHECK/CHECK/INSIST); only these three conversions are not, so a malformed record derived from attacker-sized key material enters the security-critical trust store, corrupting RFC5011 trust-anchor state and likely causing a downstream assertion failure.

evidence.reason: Unchecked failure sentinel reaching a security-critical write sink. dns_rdata_fromstruct() marshals attacker-derived keydata (converted from the fetched DNSKEY at line 526 via dns_keydata_fromdnskey) into the 4096-byte key_buf; when the marshalled KEYDATA exceeds the buffer the call fails, but its return value is discarded (no CHECK/RUNTIME_CHECK/INSIST/if anywhere between the call and the sink), so the invalid keydatarr is passed to update_one_rr() and committed to the managed-keys trust-anchor zone. Instantiated trigger: remotely fetched DNSKEY RRset whose RRSIG verifies with a currently trusted key (secure = true, line 152) plus one new KSK-flagged DNSKEY with rdata > 4096 bytes (DNS rdata permits up to 65535), reaching the newkey branch (line 475). The same defect appears at lines 284-286 and 514-516.

Origin of the tainted value: kfetch->dnskeyset is the DNSKEY RRset fetched over the network for managed-keys maintenance (untrusted origin; the code itself re-validates it with dns_dnssec_verify and resets its trust to dns_trust_none at line 101). The attacker-controlled DNSKEY rdata of unbounded size (up to ~65 KB) enters here and flows through dns_keydata_fromdnskey (line 526) into keydata, whose marshalled size is never checked against the 4096-byte key_buf before the update_one_rr write.

assumptions: isc_buffer_init(&keyb, key_buf, sizeof(key_buf)) bounds writes into key_buf, so an oversized KEYDATA surfaces as a conversion failure (e.g. ISC_R_NOSPACE) leaving keydatarr in a non-marshalled state rather than overflowing the stack buffer; the exact post-failure field values inside dns_rdata_fromstruct are not shown.

The downstream behavior of update_one_rr/dns_difftuple_create/zone_journal (crash vs. stored malformed record) is not shown; the confirmed defect is the unchecked use of the failed conversion's output at this code's own write sink.

matchkey() (callee not shown) is assumed to leave the keydataset cursor positioned at the matching record so that dns_rdataset_current at line 352 retrieves the matching keydata; no quotable contract exists in the given code.
DNS rdata lengths up to 65535 bytes permit DNSKEY rdata larger than 4096 bytes (protocol fact, not a code statement).
limitations: dns_db_detachnode(devent->db, &devent->node) at line 43 would dereference a NULL db if node were non-NULL while db were NULL, but no statement in this code can produce that state — speculative.
zone->refreshkeycount-- (line 66) could underflow only if the counter were already 0; no producing statement in this code instantiates that — speculative.

The precise consequence inside the not-shown update_one_rr consumer (assertion failure/crash vs. a stored zero-length or truncated KEYDATA record corrupting RFC5011 add/remove hold-down timers) could not be quoted from the given code; the vulnerability finding rests on the unchecked failure reaching the trust-database write in this function.

verdict.summary: smacker_read_header parses an untrusted file and reads the attacker-controlled frame count (smk->frames = get_le32(pb)). The only guard, if(smk->frames > 0xFFFFFF), merely logs an error with no return, so oversized frame counts fall through to smk->frm_size = av_malloc(smk->frames * 4), where the signed 32-bit multiplication overflows and wraps to a tiny allocation (e.g. frames=0x40000001 gives a 4-byte buffer). The following fill loop for(i=0; i<smk->frames; i++) smk->frm_size[i] = get_le32(pb) then writes attacker-controlled file content far past the end of the heap buffer, an out-of-bounds heap write with attacker-scalable magnitude. The av_malloc results are also never checked for NULL.

evidence.reason: Root cause: integer overflow in allocation sizing (CWE-190). The 'Too many frames' guard only calls av_log and contains no return, so an attacker-supplied frames value of 0x40000001 flows into av_malloc(smk->frames * 4), where the product wraps to 4 bytes; the fill loop then runs 0x40000001 iterations writing get_le32(pb) values (attacker file content) out of bounds past the 4-byte heap block — heap buffer overflow with attacker-controlled data and attacker-scalable magnitude.

evidence.snippet: smk->frames = get_le32(pb);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted sizing value: the frame count is read directly from the untrusted input file with no validation, and it later reaches the overflowed allocation size and loop bound.

assumptions: The SmackerContext struct fields (frames, treesize, pts_inc) are 32-bit ints; the struct definition is not shown, but the code's own explicit casts such as (int32_t)get_le32(pb) and the int arithmetic smk->frames * 4 indicate 32-bit width.

av_malloc's exact signature and whether it internally rejects huge/zero sizes are not shown; no such enforcement can be quoted, so none is relied upon — the trigger uses a size (4 bytes) that any allocator accepts.
limitations: smk->pts_inc = -smk->pts_inc overflows at INT32_MIN and smk->pts_inc *= 100 overflows for large values; the corrupted value only feeds av_reduce/av_set_pts_info (timebase computation) whose harmful use is not shown in this code.

The magic check at line 10 has no consequence (no return shown), so non-SMK files are parsed; no memory-safety impact by itself.

frm_flags = av_malloc(smk->frames) and its fill loop are size-consistent for positive frames; if the allocation fails and returns NULL, the unchecked loop would NULL-deref, but this is secondary to the confirmed frm_size overflow.

verdict.summary: Heap buffer overflow (out-of-bounds write) in DRMSource::read. In the AVC/NAL path the destination pointer dstData = src = (*buffer)->data() + (*buffer)->range_offset() is displaced range_offset() bytes into the buffer, but the write-bound check 'dstOffset + 4 + nalLength > (*buffer)->size()' (lines 79-81) validates dstOffset only against size() as if writes began at data(). With any non-zero range offset the start-code writes (lines 91-94) and memcpy (line 95) can write up to range_offset()+size() absolute bytes, overflowing the allocation by up to range_offset() bytes with attacker-controlled decrypted media content (e.g. size()=1000, range_offset()=500 permits writes at data()[1000..1499]). The non-AVC else path (line 104) performs memcpy(src, decryptedDrmBuffer.data, decryptedDrmBuffer.length) with no destination bound at all. All triggering values (range_offset, range_length, size, NAL lengths, decrypted content) are attacker-data from the media file entering at mOriginalMediaSource->read; no statement in this code validates them against the write position.

evidence.reason: Defective bound (missing-check site): this guard runs on every iteration before the sink, but it bounds dstOffset+4+nalLength against (*buffer)->size() as measured from data(), while dstData already points range_offset() bytes past data() (lines 10 and 34). Edge test: at range_offset()==0 the check is exact; at any range_offset()>0 it still permits dstOffset+4+nalLength == size(), i.e. absolute writes up to range_offset()+size(), out of bounds by up to range_offset() bytes. No statement anywhere in the function adds the range_offset() term.

Sink of the primary candidate (CWE-787): these writes index dstData, which equals data()+range_offset(), with indices the guard at lines 79-81 allows up to size(). Simulated trigger: size()=1000, range_offset()=500, range_length()=500, mNALLengthSize=1, 2-byte NALs; at dstOffset=995, nalLength=1 the guard passes (995+4+1=1000 not > 1000) and the writes land at data()[1495..1499], 500 bytes past the 1000-byte allocation, with attacker-controlled NAL payload bytes — memory corruption.

evidence.snippet: char *src = (char *)(*buffer)->data() + (*buffer)->range_offset();
evidence.reason: Origin of the taint: range_offset() is attacker-data returned by mOriginalMediaSource->read (media-file content, line 4) and enters here; via line 34 (uint8_t *dstData = (uint8_t*)src) it displaces every subsequent dstData[...] write and memcpy destination, invalidating the size()-relative bound at line 81. No statement in this code constrains range_offset() to 0 or folds it into any bound.

Second sink sharing the root cause (CWE-787): the non-AVC path copies decryptedDrmBuffer.length bytes to src = data()+range_offset() with NO bounds check of any form anywhere on this path — neither range_offset()+length vs (*buffer)->size(), nor a check that the decrypt callee (which receives DrmBuffer** at lines 18-19 and can mutate .length, unchecked by the pointer-identity CHECK at line 28) left length within the destination's remaining extent. Any buffer with range_offset()+length > size() (or a callee-enlarged length) overflows the allocation.

assumptions: (*buffer)->size() is treated as the allocated byte extent starting at (*buffer)->data(); this is the capacity model the code itself uses in its bound at line 81. No statement in the given code documents MediaBuffer's memory layout.

mNALLengthSize, mWantsNALFragments, mDecryptHandle and mTrackId are members whose producing statements are outside the given code and could not be quoted; they are not relied upon to dismiss any candidate.

The upstream media source and the DRM plugin are the intake point for media-file content; no 'range_offset is always 0' or 'callee preserves length' contract is quotable from this code, so those values are treated as attacker-data.
limitations: Candidate C (speculative): mDrmManagerClient->decrypt receives DrmBuffer** and may enlarge decryptedDrmBuffer.length beyond the new char[len] allocation made at line 15; that would make the reads at line 42 and the memcpy source at line 95 out of bounds (CWE-125) and amplify the line 104 overflow. The mutating statement lives in a callee not shown, so per STEP 4(a) the trigger could not be instantiated from quoted statements.

Candidate D (not instantiated as in-code impact): a truncated access unit with len < mNALLengthSize fails CHECK at line 40 (e.g. len=1, mNALLengthSize=4) and mNALLengthSize outside 1..4 hits CHECK(!"Should not be here.") at line 58; both abort. The process-termination behavior executes inside the CHECK macro (framework code not given), so the impact chain is not instantiated in this code; if CHECK aborts a shared privileged media process, this is an attacker-reachable denial of service.

verdict.summary: No instantiated vulnerability. The attacker-influenced read() return (count, 0..1010) is guarded by 'if (count < 0) ... return;' before first use, and buf is always NUL-terminated in bounds by 'buf[count + 14 < BUF_SIZE ? count + 14 : BUF_SIZE - 1] = '\0';' on the only path to 'strcpy(out, buf)'. At the exactly-at-limit case (count = 1010) the terminator lands at buf[1023], giving strlen(buf) <= 1023 and a strcpy of at most 1024 bytes into the 1024-byte out buffer — no overflow. The sole caller passes equal 1024-byte buffers and a literal BUF_SIZE, so no mismatched-size or negative-remaining trigger is reachable. Residual non-security issues: fd is not closed on the success path (one descriptor per process, not attacker-scalable), and a short read or oversized file merely truncates the echoed output.

assumptions: argv values (filename, type) are supplied by the same user who runs the process; no setuid/daemon context is quotable from the given code, so filename is treated as user-controlled content but with no privilege boundary to cross.
read() obeys POSIX semantics: returns at most the requested count (remaining = BUF_SIZE - 14 = 1010), which bounds count to [0,1010] after the quoted negative check.

The relationship 'out and buf are each at least BUF_SIZE bytes' is a contract enforced by the shown caller's declarations 'char buf[BUF_SIZE];' and 'char out[BUF_SIZE];' with 'const int BUF_SIZE = 1024;' — quoted from the given code, not assumed.
limitations: File descriptor leak: on the success path, copy_file_content returns after 'strcpy(out, buf);' without close(fd). One leaked fd per call; main calls the function once and exits, so no attacker-scalable retention — not classified as a security vulnerability.

Single read() call: a short read or a file larger than 1010 bytes truncates the echoed content to at most 1023 bytes. Cosmetic output truncation only; the terminator index is derived from count, so memory safety is unaffected.

copy_file_content as a non-static function would be unsafe if a future caller passed buffers smaller than BUF_SIZE or BUF_SIZE <= 14 (making 'remaining' negative), but the only call site in the given code passes literal 1024 with equal-size buffers, so no such trigger is instantiable here.

verdict.summary: saveSecreteFile violates its documented contract that the secret file 'should be accessible only by the current user': it sets umask(0022) before creating the file with std::ofstream, which on POSIX creates the file with mode 0666 & ~0022 = 0644. The resulting secret file is group-readable and world-readable, disclosing its secret content to any other local user able to traverse the directory. No chmod/fchmod/restrictive-umask statement exists anywhere in the code to enforce the claimed owner-only permission.

evidence.reason: Root cause: umask(0022) clears only group-write and other-write bits. std::ofstream creates a new file with base mode 0666, yielding 0666 & ~0022 = 0644 (rw-r--r--), so the 'secret' file is readable by all other local users, contradicting both the documented contract ('accessible only by the current user') and the inline comment ('others have no permissions', which would require umask 0007 for the claimed 660). Trigger fully instantiated: main passes argv[1..3], the emptiness check on line 16 passes for any non-empty inputs, filepath is built on line 22, and line 28 creates the world-readable file containing the secret content written on line 36. No chmod, fchmod, restrictive umask, or post-creation permission check exists on any path in this code.

assumptions: On POSIX with a typical C++ standard library (libstdc++/libc++), std::ofstream creates a nonexistent file via open(path, O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC, 0666); the effective mode is therefore 0666 & ~0022 = 0644. This standard-library creation mode is not visible in the given code.

The deployment privilege level of the process is unknown from the code; the impact (other local users reading the secret) assumes a multi-user host, which is the environment the documented 'current user only' contract implies.
limitations: Path traversal: filename containing '/' or '..' escapes the directory (no canonicalization; the only guard quoted is the emptiness check on line 16). However, the only visible caller is main passing user-supplied argv to a process running as that same user, so no cross-trust-boundary write impact is instantiable from the given code.

Symlink following: std::ofstream does not use O_NOFOLLOW, so a pre-existing symlink at filepath would be followed and truncated; exploiting this requires an attacker-planted filesystem object at a path this code never makes attacker-writable — speculative per STEP 4.
umask(0022) temporarily mutates process-global state (lines 25–45); in a multithreaded caller this would race, but no threads exist in the given code.
file.close() return value is unchecked (line 44); write failure is caught at line 37, so this has no security effect.

verdict.summary: The decoder init function NULL-checks both allocation results (av_frame_alloc at line 7, av_fast_malloc at line 11), so every allocation-failure path returns AVERROR(ENOMEM) instead of continuing. The only attacker-data input is avctx->width (container-controlled, never validated in this code), and it feeds exactly one sink: the allocation size 's->avctx->width * sizeof(unsigned int)' at line 10, which is unguarded. On ILP32 targets a width >= 2^30 wraps the size_t product (e.g. width 0x40000001 yields size 4), producing a drastically undersized vert_pred buffer that passes the NULL check and init reports success. However, the harmful use of that buffer (out-of-bounds indexing in the truemotion1 decode routine) does not occur anywhere in the given code, and on LP64 targets the int-to-size_t multiplication cannot wrap for any int width; the trigger and impact chain are therefore not instantiated within this code, and the defect is recorded as a limitation rather than a finding.

assumptions: avctx and avctx->priv_data are non-NULL and priv_data is zero-initialized by the calling framework; no statement in this code asserts or checks this (line 3 dereferences avctx unconditionally).

av_fast_malloc sets *ptr to NULL on allocation failure and performs no allocation for a size of 0, so the check 'if (!s->vert_pred)' at line 11 catches allocation failure; this is callee behavior not quotable from the given code.
avctx->width is set by the demuxer/container layer outside this code; per discipline 3 it is treated as attacker-data, not contract.
limitations: Integer overflow / buffer size miscalculation (CWE-190 / CWE-131): 'av_fast_malloc(&s->vert_pred, &s->vert_pred_size, s->avctx->width * sizeof(unsigned int));' (line 10) performs an unvalidated, unchecked int-to-size_t multiplication. On a 32-bit size_t platform, width = 0x40000001 makes the product wrap to 4, allocating a tiny non-NULL buffer while the NULL check at line 11 passes and init returns success. The trigger preconditions that could not be instantiated in this code are: (a) an ILP32 target (on LP64 the product cannot wrap for any int width, max ~8.59e9 < 2^64), and (b) the out-of-bounds write itself, which would occur in the truemotion1 decode function that indexes s->vert_pred by column — that function is not given, so the impact chain breaks outside this code. The upstream fix (validating dimensions, e.g. av_image_check_size) is absent from this code.

Memory leak: on the early 'return AVERROR(ENOMEM);' at line 12, s->frame (allocated at line 6) is not freed. This is reachable only on allocation failure (environment), leaks a single fixed-size frame per init call, and has no attacker-scalable retention or security effect.

Missing dimension validation: no check on avctx->width exists anywhere in this code; width <= 0 values produce size 0 or a huge wrapped size, both of which this code converts into an ENOMEM return via the quoted NULL checks, so no bad-dimension state is presented as success within this function.

verdict.summary: copy_file_content reads file content into buf+14 without ever NUL-terminating it, then calls strcpy(out, buf). In 'security' mode main pads buf[14..1023] with 0x07 (overwriting snprintf's terminator), and in both modes a read of 1010 NUL-free bytes fills the entire buffer with attacker data — leaving no NUL byte in buf's 1024 bytes. strcpy then scans past the end of buf (out-of-bounds read) and writes past the end of the 1024-byte stack buffer out (out-of-bounds write), a stack buffer overflow with attacker-influenced content; the sole post-hoc statement out[BUF_SIZE-1]='\0' runs after the overflow and terminates out, not buf.

evidence.reason: read() never NUL-terminates buf; the only check between the read and the sink is `if (count < 0)` (error sentinel only). No statement writes buf[14+count]='\0', clamps the length, or uses a bounds-safe copy. strcpy(out, buf) then requires a NUL within buf[0..1023], which does not exist when main pads with 0x07 (empty or short file in 'security' mode) or when the file supplies 1010 NUL-free bytes (either mode): the source scan runs past buf[1023] (out-of-bounds read) and the copy writes past out[1023] (out-of-bounds stack write). Instantiated trigger: ./a.out <attacker file> security with an empty file — count=0, buf = "File content: " + 1010 bytes of 0x07, strcpy overflows the 1024-byte stack buffer out.

Origin of the unterminated source: memset(buf + 14, 7, BUF_SIZE - 14) fills buf[14..1023] with the non-zero byte 0x07, destroying the NUL that snprintf(buf, sizeof(buf), "File content: ") placed at buf[14]. Combined with read() not appending a terminator, buf contains no NUL byte at all when the file is empty or shorter than 1010 bytes, making the strcpy at line 29 unbounded.

assumptions: The deployment context (CLI tool vs. setuid binary) is not quotable from the given code; per discipline 3 the file content read at line 21 and the argv values are treated as untrusted attacker-data regardless.
Exact stack layout (whether a stack canary or adjacent locals are hit first) is compiler-dependent and not shown; the corruption itself is instantiated by line 29 alone.
limitations: File descriptor fd is never closed on the success path (no close(fd) after line 29) — a resource leak with no memory-safety, bypass, or amplification chain in this code; not counted as a vulnerability.
If the file content contains an embedded NUL, strcpy stops early and out receives only a prefix of the file content — a correctness/cosmetic truncation, not a security impact.

A correct fix would need remaining = BUF_SIZE - 15 plus an explicit buf[14+count] = '\0' (terminating at buf[1024] would itself be out of bounds); no such statement exists in any form anywhere in the given code.

verdict.summary: All memory-access sinks in this Mach-O chained-fixup iterator are guarded by quoted, execution-order-verified checks: segment/starts indexing is bounded by 'i < bin->nsegs && i < bin->segs_count', page_start indexing is bounded by 'if (page_idx >= bin->chained_starts[i]->page_count) break;' plus a NULL check before the access, page_size division is protected by 'if (page_size < 1) page_size = 4096;', and the attacker-controlled cursor is only used through r_buf_read_at whose failure sentinel is checked before the data is consumed. Remaining OOB/termination candidates depend on array-allocation sizes, dyld bitfield widths, and r_buf_read_at's internal bounds behavior, none of which are quotable from the given code.

The dyld chained-pointer bitfield widths (e.g., p->next) are small enough that 'delta * stride' cannot wrap to 0 with delta != 0 (would need a next field >= 61 bits); struct definitions are external headers not quotable here.

limitations: Unsigned underflow in the callback gate: 'cursor <= limit_end - 8' evaluates to a huge value when limit_end < 8 (ut64 wrap), so the callback can fire for cursors whose 8-byte entry extends up to 7 bytes past limit_end; the enclosing 'while (cursor < limit_end && cursor < end)' still bounds cursor, and the only consequence in this code is passing an out-of-window offset to the not-shown callback — impact chain not instantiated (CWE-191 pattern, not confirmable as a vulnerability here).

verdict.summary: trim_spaces() indexes str[len - 1] without checking len > 0. When the string is empty (argv[1] = "") or consists entirely of spaces, len reaches 0 and the loop reads (and conditionally writes) one byte before the heap allocation at str[-1], corrupting heap metadata if that byte is 0x20 and then scanning further backwards (len becomes -1, -2, ...). The caller validates only argc, not the string's emptiness, so the trigger is fully attacker-controlled via the command-line argument.

evidence.reason: The loop reads str[len - 1] with no check that len > 0. For input "" (or an all-spaces string), len = strlen(str) = 0, so str[-1] is read out of bounds before the malloc'd buffer; if that heap byte equals ' ', str[-1] = '\0' performs an out-of-bounds write into heap metadata and len-- drives a backward scan over memory beyond the allocation. No bounds, clamp, or empty-string check exists on any path.

Attacker-controlled argv[1] (only argc < 2 is checked, never emptiness) is copied into the heap buffer buf2 and passed to trim_spaces, instantiating the trigger: an empty or all-space argument makes len reach 0 inside trim_spaces, reaching the out-of-bounds str[len - 1] access.

assumptions: Command-line arguments are treated as untrusted input per the data-origin model; the program's deployment context (CLI) was not used to demote or promote any candidate.

The heap byte at buf2[-1] is implementation-specific; on typical glibc heaps it is the chunk size field (0x21), so the guaranteed impact is the out-of-bounds read, with the out-of-bounds write and backward scan occurring when that byte is 0x20.
limitations: int len = strlen(str) truncates size_t to int (CWE-190/191 candidate), but strings near INT_MAX cannot reach line 8 through this code's actual input surface (execve ARG_MAX bounds argv[1]); trigger not instantiated — speculative.

malloc return values (lines 25-27) are unchecked, so strcpy(buf2, ...) could dereference NULL, but this requires an allocation failure no attacker can induce through this input surface; not classified as a vulnerability.
buf1 is allocated and freed without ever being used (CWE-457-like); no uninitialized value reaches output or control flow, so no security effect.

Residual concerns (headerGet/headerPut/rpmtdFreeData internal behavior, sigh blob consistency produced by not-shown import code, msg non-NULL contract) could not be instantiated as triggers from statements in this code and are recorded as limitations.

The error message text 'invalid signature tag' is also emitted when the loop breaks because the target tag already exists in the main header (headerIsEntry path); it still reports failure via a non-zero return and msg, so this is cosmetic wording, not security-state misrepresentation.

Worst-case bounded amplification: a count of exactly 16777216 (the allowed limit) multiplied by element size yields a large but attacker-input-proportional copy; the count gate caps it and the loop breaks on the first failed check, so no unbounded consumption exists.

verdict.summary: dxa_read_packet discards the return values of avio_read for the tag (line 22), palette (line 37), and frame-header (line 40) reads. On short or failed reads the stack buffers buf[DXA_EXTRA_SIZE] and pal[768+4] remain partially or fully uninitialized, yet all their bytes are copied verbatim into the returned AVPacket (memcpy at lines 28/29/48/54). A crafted, truncated DXA stream (e.g. 'FRAM' + 5 header bytes + EOF, giving size=0 so the line-50 check passes) makes the demuxer return packets containing uninitialized stack memory, disclosing it through the demuxer's output; the CMAP path scales the disclosure to ~763 bytes. Uninitialized data also feeds the AV_RL32 tag dispatch (line 23) and the size computation (line 41).

evidence.reason: Root cause: the return value of avio_read at line 40 is unchecked, so a short/failed read leaves buf[9..15] uninitialized while memcpy at line 48 copies all DXA_EXTRA_SIZE bytes of buf into the packet. Instantiated trigger: file = 'FRAM' + 5 bytes 00 00 00 00 00 then EOF; avio_read returns 5 (discarded), size = AV_RB32(buf[5..8]) = 0 passes the line-42 check, av_new_packet(pkt,16) succeeds, memcpy copies 7 uninitialized stack bytes into pkt->data, avio_read(...,0) returns 0 == size so the line-50 check passes, and the packet carrying uninitialized stack memory is returned at line 59.

assumptions: c->frames, c->has_sound, c->bytes_left, c->bpc, c->vidpos are populated from the file header by a read_header function not shown; the loop condition 'while(!url_feof(s->pb) && c->frames)' only requires frames > 0, which attacker-controlled header content can satisfy.

DXA_EXTRA_SIZE is assumed to be 16 (the dxa.h constant), making the FRAM header read DXA_EXTRA_SIZE - 4 = 12 bytes into buf[4..15]; all offsets used (buf+5, buf+4) are in-bounds of buf[16] regardless.

Refuted: out-of-bounds write via pal_size — pal_size is only ever 0 (line 7) or 768+4 (line 35), and pal is declared 'pal[768+4]', so the memcpys at lines 28/29/48/54 stay in-bounds of the allocation '4 + pal_size' / 'size + DXA_EXTRA_SIZE + pal_size'.
Refuted: unsigned-signed confusion at 'ret != size' (line 50) — a negative avio_read error converts to a huge unsigned value that fails the equality check and takes the EIO path.

Speculative: dispatching on fully-uninitialized AV_RL32(buf) on the first iteration (line 23) matching a known tag by chance is possible but not attacker-deterministically instantiable; it is subsumed by the confirmed uninitialized-memory finding, not counted as a separate trigger.
The exact stack contents disclosed depend on prior stack state; the disclosure channel is the packet data itself, which is this function's direct output.

limitations: Functional defect (trigger fully instantiated, impact outside given code): line 13 computes 'fp48_pck(t, a);' but lines 14-17 serialize 'a[0][1], a[0][2], a[1][0], a[1][2]' instead of the packed 't'.
