Any security consequence (fp48_read_bin/upk reconstructing a different group element, failed verification of serialized G_T material, integrity failures) requires consumer code not given, so this is a round-trip/correctness bug (fail-closed), recorded here rather than as a vulnerability of this code.

NULL-dereference candidate on 'bin': no non-NULL check exists in the code, but triggering it requires the caller to pass NULL with an exactly matching 'len'; worst case is a process crash with no corruption or disclosure, and it is not attacker-content driven — not treated as a finding.

verdict.summary: The classic risk for this pattern — XPath injection — is structurally absent: the XPath expression is the compile-time constant "//student", and the attacker-supplied username/password are only compared via short-circuit-guarded strcmp, never interpolated into the query. Remaining defects (missing NULL check on xpath_obj->nodesetval before nodeset->nodeNr, strdup(content) without a NULL test, printf("%s") on potentially-NULL StudentInfo fields, and free() used where xmlFree() is contractually required for xmlNodeGetContent results) all either depend on not-shown libxml2 version/allocator behavior or terminate at an unquoted libc link, so no candidate survives as a primary vulnerability in this code.

decrypt_response parses a cipher length directly from the untrusted card-response buffer (in[1..in[3], up to 0xFFFF via 'in_len = in[2] * 0x100; in_len += in[3];') and passes it, minus one, as the decryption length into a fixed 4096-byte stack buffer 'plaintext' (aes128_decrypt_cbc/des3_decrypt_cbc). No statement anywhere bounds in_len against sizeof(plaintext) or a minimum value, so a malicious card response with in[1]=0x82 and in[2]/in[3] encoding any length > 4096 causes an out-of-bounds stack write of thousands of attacker-scaled bytes (and in_len=0 underflows to SIZE_MAX). The same unvalidated in_len also drives out-of-bounds reads in the unpadding loop (plaintext[in_len-2] with in_len==1 indexing SIZE_MAX) and in memcpy(out, plaintext, in_len - 2).

evidence.reason: Sink: attacker-controlled in_len (0..0xFFFF from the card response) minus one is used as the CBC decryption length writing into the fixed 4096-byte stack buffer 'plaintext' declared at line 6. No bound check on in_len exists on any path (STEP 5 search found none), so a response with in[1]=0x82, in[2]=0x20, in[3]=0x00, in[4]=0x01 gives in_len=8192 and writes 8191 bytes into a 4096-byte stack array — out-of-bounds stack write (memory corruption); in_len=0 makes in_len-1 underflow to SIZE_MAX.

Taint origin: the two-byte length field is composed from attacker bytes in[2] and in[3], yielding in_len up to 0xFFFF (65535) with no upper bound relative to the 4096-byte destination buffer or any minimum bound; this value flows directly to the decrypt sink at lines 37-40.

evidence.snippet:
while (0x80 != plaintext[in_len - 2] && (in_len - 2 > 0))
		in_len--;
evidence.reason: Corollary of the same unvalidated in_len: with in_len==1 the unsigned expression in_len-2 wraps to SIZE_MAX and indexes plaintext[SIZE_MAX] (out-of-bounds read) because the guard (in_len - 2 > 0) is evaluated after the index read and is true for the wrapped value; with large in_len it reads plaintext far past the 4096-byte buffer.

evidence.snippet:
memcpy(out, plaintext, in_len - 2);
	*out_len = in_len - 2;
evidence.reason: Corollary sink: copies in_len-2 bytes (attacker-scaled, potentially up to ~65533) out of the 4096-byte plaintext buffer with no bound against sizeof(plaintext) and no knowledge of the capacity of 'out', producing an out-of-bounds read of plaintext and a potential overflow of the caller's output buffer.

assumptions: The buffer 'in' is assumed to contain at least 5 readable bytes; the function signature provides no length parameter for 'in', so this code cannot verify it (and the decrypt calls read up to in_len-1 bytes from 'in', which may exceed 'in's real allocation — same missing-validation root cause).

exdata->sk_enc and exdata->smtype are assumed to have been initialized by driver setup code not shown; whether the attacker knows the session key (and thus controls the overflowing plaintext content) is unknown, but the overflow length is attacker-controlled regardless.

aes128_decrypt_cbc/des3_decrypt_cbc are assumed to have standard decrypt-into-buffer semantics (write 'length' bytes to the destination); this code supplies both the destination (4096-byte stack array) and the attacker-derived length.
'out' and 'out_len' are assumed non-NULL per an unstated caller contract; no check exists in this code.
limitations: Overflow of the caller's 'out' buffer at memcpy (line 49) cannot be sized because 'out's capacity is not given; the out-of-bounds READ of plaintext at that memcpy is, however, fully instantiated.

in_len == 0 underflow (in_len - 1 == SIZE_MAX passed as decryption length) requires the callee to treat such a length literally to manifest the write; it is included as a variant of the same missing-bound defect, which is already primary via the plain oversized-length trigger.
'card' itself is dereferenced (card->drv_data) without a NULL check on card; triggerable only by a malformed internal caller, not by card data, so not counted as a finding.
Whether the process runs privileged (e.g., as a pkcs11 module in a privileged application) is a deployment assumption; per discipline 3 it is not used to set or demote severity.

verdict.summary: decrypt_response copies cipher_len - 2 bytes (up to 4094) of attacker-influenced plaintext into the caller's out buffer via memcpy without any check of out's capacity: the function never receives or reads out's size, and the only length guard (cipher_len < 2 || i+cipher_len > inlen || cipher_len > sizeof plaintext) bounds the length only against inlen and the local plaintext[4096], never against the destination. A malicious card's response (in[1]=0x82, in[2..3] giving a large length, in[4]=0x01) fully controls the copy length and, via the decrypted padding byte, its stopping point, producing a buffer overflow with attacker-controlled length and content.

evidence.reason: The sink memcpy(out, plaintext, cipher_len - 2) writes up to 4094 attacker-influenced bytes into out, whose capacity is never passed to, read by, or checked against anywhere in this function. Trigger fully instantiated: card response {0x00,0x82,0x10,0x00,0x01,...} with inlen=4101 yields cipher_len=4096 (passes the check at line 37 since 5+4096==4101<=inlen and 4096 is not > sizeof plaintext), the attacker-chosen plaintext padding byte 0x80 stops the unpadding loop immediately at cipher_len=4096, the '2 == cipher_len' early-out does not fire, and memcpy copies 4094 bytes into an unbounded destination — memory corruption with attacker-controlled length and content.

Origin of the faulty value: cipher_len is computed entirely from attacker-controlled card-response bytes in[2] and in[3] (range 0..65535). The subsequent guard at line 37 clamps it only to [2, 4096] against inlen and the local plaintext buffer; no statement ever relates it to the capacity of out, so the attacker selects the memcpy length at line 53.

assumptions: The out buffer's actual capacity is not shown in the given code; the signature passes no capacity for it, so the code cannot have checked it — the defect is the unchecked copy in this function, judged as the last line of defense for the card-response data it decodes.
exdata->sk_enc / exdata->smtype are set outside this function; no statement here prevents later mutation, but they only select the cipher and key and do not bound any length.
aes128_decrypt_cbc / des3_decrypt_cbc are not shown; taken to write cipher_len - 1 (<= 4095) bytes into plaintext[4096], which the quoted guard at line 37 keeps in bounds.
limitations: Out-of-bounds READ candidate: in[2], in[3], in[4] are read during header parsing (lines 20, 24, 28) before any inlen check — the only inlen guard (line 37) executes after the parse. A response with inlen < 5 whose prefix matches a branch reads past inlen. Not promoted to primary because the physical size of the caller's receive buffer is not shown, so the actual out-of-bounds memory access could not be instantiated in this code.
out_len is dereferenced (*out_len = cipher_len - 2) without a NULL check; reachability requires a caller passing NULL, which is not shown.
The unpadding while-loop was edge-tested at cipher_len == 2 (index plaintext[0], second conjunct fails) and shown not to underflow.

verdict.summary: l2_allocate uses the caller-supplied signed int l1_index to index the heap-allocated L1 table with no bounds check anywhere in the function: line 8 performs s->l1_table[l1_index] (out-of-bounds read) and line 15 performs s->l1_table[l1_index] = l2_offset | QCOW_OFLAG_COPIED (out-of-bounds 8-byte heap write at an attacker-chosen scaled offset, reachable at any negative or >= s->l1_size index). The only guards present (l2_offset < 0, write_l1_entry < 0, byte-count comparisons) test other values, so the index reaches both sinks unvalidated on the single execution path.

evidence.snippet: static uint64_t *l2_allocate(BlockDriverState *bs, int l1_index)
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: the signed 32-bit index l1_index enters as a parameter with no documented, asserted, or checked precondition anywhere in the given code, so it is classified attacker-data; nothing between this line and its uses constrains it.

evidence.snippet: old_l2_offset = s->l1_table[l1_index];
evidence.reason: First sink: out-of-bounds READ of s->l1_table (a uint64_t array sized s->l1_size) at the unvalidated index; executes before any check in the function, so no guard can precede it. Leaked heap content flows into old_l2_offset and is later used as a file-read offset.

evidence.snippet:
s->l1_table[l1_index] = l2_offset | QCOW_OFLAG_COPIED;
    if (write_l1_entry(s, l1_index) < 0) {
evidence.reason: Primary defect: out-of-bounds 8-byte heap WRITE into s->l1_table at the attacker-chosen index (l1_index negative or >= s->l1_size; signed int gives a roughly +/-16 GB reach around the allocation). The adjacent check on line 16 tests write_l1_entry's return value, not l1_index, and the earlier l2_offset < 0 check tests the allocation result, so the write is unguarded on the only path reaching it.

assumptions: The caller of this static helper is not shown; any real-world bounding of l1_index (e.g., block-layer offset clamping or L1-table growth at the call site) cannot be quoted from the given code and per GUARD ANCHORING was treated as absent rather than as a guard.
bs is treated as a non-NULL driver-state interface pointer (line 3 deref); it carries no data content and a NULL would only crash, so it was not treated as a data-carrying attacker input.

The return range of l2_cache_new_entry (line 20), the header validation of s->l2_bits and s->l2_size at image open, and the BDRVQcowState field semantics all live in code not given and are unverifiable assumptions.

qcow2_alloc_clusters' failure sentinel is negative, which line 11 does check (l2_offset < 0); offset 0 was assumed a valid in-range allocation result since no sentinel for 0 appears in the given code.
limitations: Fail-open metadata ordering (historical qcow2 defect): lines 15-16 commit s->l1_table[l1_index] and the on-disk L1 entry to the newly allocated cluster marked QCOW_OFLAG_COPIED BEFORE the cluster is initialized; the error returns at lines 17, 30 and 36 then leave the in-memory and on-disk L1 entry permanently pointing to an uninitialized cluster and leave the cache slot min_index holding new table data while s->l2_cache_offsets[min_index] (line 38) is never updated. The corrupted state is produced entirely by this code, but its consumption (stale bytes interpreted as L2 entries redirecting guest I/O, cache offset/buffer mismatch) occurs in code not given, so the impact chain is not instantiated here.

Speculative: if l2_cache_new_entry could return a failure sentinel (e.g., -1), line 21 would compute s->l2_cache + (-1 << s->l2_bits) and line 24 memset would write out of bounds before the cache; the callee is not shown so this trigger cannot be instantiated.

Speculative: min_index << s->l2_bits can overflow signed int and s->l2_size * sizeof(uint64_t) can overflow if the unshown header parser accepts extreme l2_bits/l2_size values from a crafted image; no producing or validating statement exists in this code.

The old_l2_offset value read at line 8 originates from attacker-supplied qcow2 image content and can carry flag bits (bit 63) into the bdrv_pread offset at line 27; direct impact is confined to the attacker's own image file, and the resulting error path folds into the ordering defect recorded above.

Cluster leak: on every error return after a successful qcow2_alloc_clusters the allocated cluster is never released; this requires I/O failure the attacker cannot reliably induce and has no corruption, disclosure, bypass, or amplification effect.

verdict.summary: All identified defects in split() — the `if (!tmp && result)` check that misses the first-iteration realloc failure (NULL-pointer write at `result[i++]`), the double free of `copy` in the final realloc error path after it was already freed, and the unchecked dupstr results — are gated exclusively on allocation failure that cannot be deterministically induced by any attacker-controlled value this code processes (the first realloc is a fixed 8-byte request; the final realloc is smaller than memory already successfully held). No guard-bypass, corruption, injection, or amplification trigger is instantiable from the given code, so no vulnerability is confirmed; the OOM-path robustness bugs are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: dupstr(arg) behaves like strdup (allocates strlen(arg)+1 bytes and can return NULL on allocation failure); its body is not shown
Callers of split() pass NUL-terminated strings and can handle a NULL return; no such contract is quotable from the given code
dupstr(cptr) can fail and return NULL; consequences for array consumers are outside this code
limitations: First-iteration realloc failure is mishandled: `if (!tmp && result)` is false when result==NULL, so `result = tmp` sets NULL and `result[i++] = dupstr(cptr)` writes through a NULL pointer (CWE-476) — trigger requires an 8-byte malloc to fail, not attacker-inducible

Double free of `copy`: freed at `free(copy)` before the `if (i)` block and freed again in the `if (!tmp)` error arm (CWE-415/416) — trigger requires the final realloc (8*(i+1) bytes, smaller than memory already held) to fail

Unchecked `dupstr(arg)` at `char *copy = dupstr(arg);` feeds `strtok(copy, delim)`; if dupstr returns NULL, strtok(NULL, ...) on a first call dereferences its saved-state NULL pointer — trigger requires attacker-induced memory exhaustion with 1:1 (non-amplifying) allocation cost, and dupstr's failure behavior is not shown
Unchecked `dupstr(cptr)` stored into the result array may place NULL mid-array; only consumer-side impact (not shown) would result
NULL return is ambiguous between empty/delimiter-only input (i==0) and allocation error; distinguishing them requires the caller, which is not shown
`sizeof *result * (i + 1)` would overflow int at i==INT_MAX, but reaching 2^31 tokens is impossible before memory exhaustion
strtok uses internal static state and is not thread-safe — hygiene issue with no instantiated security impact in this code

verdict.summary: This function merges attacker-controlled legacy signature-header entries into a header and validates tag range and type/count bounds for all enumerated rpm tag types. Two genuine validation gaps exist in this code: (1) the switch on td.type has no default arm, so an undefined type value (e.g., rpm's unused type slots 5 or 10) falls through with NO type check and NO count check (the td.count != 1 and td.count >= 16*1024 guards are attached only to the enumerated cases) and is passed to headerPut with an unbounded attacker-controlled count; (2) h/sigh are never NULL-checked and headerPut's return is ignored. However, every claimed harmful use (the copy/allocation in headerPut, the dereferences in headerInitIterator/headerNext/headerIsEntry) occurs entirely inside callees not given, and the consistency of td.count vs td.data is produced by the unshown headerNext. Per the impact-modeling rules, an instantiated trigger whose security consequence exists only in code not given is a limitation, not a finding; no memory, index, size, or injection sink is defective within the given statements. All in-code guards that do exist (tag range check, count checks) were edge-tested and verified on every path in execution order.

assumptions: headerNext(hi, &td) is assumed to populate td with a type/count/data triple consistent with the imported signature header; no statement in the given code enforces count-vs-data consistency (C4 rests on this unshown contract).

headerPut(h, &td, HEADERPUT_DEFAULT) is assumed to perform its own type/size validation before copying; its behavior with an unknown type (e.g., rpm type slots 5 or 10) and unbounded count cannot be quoted from the given code.
The constants HEADER_SIGBASE and HEADER_TAGBASE are assumed to delimit the intended signature-tag region; their values are not shown.
Callers are assumed to pass non-NULL h and sigh; the given code contains no NULL check, assert, or documented precondition, so the pointer non-NULL contract is an assumption, not a fact.
sigh's entry content originates from parsing untrusted package data; that provenance is inferred from the function's role (legacy-signature merging), as no parsing statements are shown.
limitations: Missing default arm in switch (td.type): an unknown/undefined type value bypasses all type and count validation and reaches headerPut with an attacker-controlled, unbounded td.count (e.g., type=5, count=0xFFFFFFFF). STEP 4 simulation reaches the headerPut call concretely, but the claimed impact (memory copy/allocation) occurs inside headerPut, which is not given, so the impact chain breaks at an unquoted link. Recorded as a real validation gap in this code, not a proven vulnerability here. Fix form searched and absent: default arm, explicit type-range check, or validated helper between the switch and headerPut.

No NULL validation of h and sigh, and the result of headerInitIterator(sigh) is unchecked; a NULL header would be dereferenced inside unshown callees. The trigger (caller passing NULL) is not instantiable from this code's own data flow, and the dereference is not in the given statements.

(void) headerPut(h, &td, HEADERPUT_DEFAULT); ignores the return value; a silently dropped signature entry could matter downstream, but both the failure conditions of headerPut and any downstream treatment of the merged header are outside the given code.

Whether the unshown header-import path can deliver an undefined type value (5 or 10) into td.type is unknown; this affects the reachability of the missing-default gap but cannot be resolved from the given code.

verdict.summary: validate_commit_metadata performs no memory-unsafe operation and is fail-closed on every attacker-controllable mismatch path: xa_metadata is NULL-initialized, a missing/mistyped value is rejected whenever require_xa_metadata is TRUE, and any present-but-mismatched xa.metadata is rejected via g_strcmp0 (line 15-16), with ref only ever used as a %s argument to a literal g_set_error format (line 19). The one substantive candidate — a commit lacking xa.metadata passing validation when the caller passes require_xa_metadata == FALSE even with non-NULL required_metadata — was confirmed to have no guard in any form in this code (STEP 5 search), but its trigger requires a caller-selected lenient policy combination that no statement here produces or forbids, and its security consequence (deploying the unvalidated commit) occurs entirely in the unshown caller; within this code the TRUE return faithfully reports the policy the caller requested. All other candidates (missing type check on commit_data, ignored g_variant_lookup return, NULL required_metadata with present xa_metadata) reduce to handled NULL paths or fail-closed over-rejection with no in-code security impact.

assumptions: GLib contract, not quotable from the given code: g_variant_get_child_value on a NULL, non-container, or zero-child commit_data is a programming error that returns NULL after a critical warning rather than corrupting memory; this code handles that NULL via 'if (commit_metadata != NULL)' at line 12.

GLib contract, not quotable from the given code: g_variant_lookup returns FALSE and leaves the out-argument untouched when the dictionary lacks the key or the value's type does not match "&s"; xa_metadata is pre-initialized NULL at line 8, so no uninitialized use results.

Callers of this non-static function are not shown; ref, required_metadata, and require_xa_metadata are treated as caller-supplied policy values, and commit_data as attacker-influenceable serialized content, per the data-origin impact model.
limitations: Fail-open candidate (not confirmed): when the caller passes require_xa_metadata == FALSE, a commit_data whose metadata lacks "xa.metadata" — or a non-container commit_data, since commit_metadata == NULL is tolerated — returns TRUE even when required_metadata is non-NULL. No statement in this code ties rejection of a missing xa.metadata to required_metadata != NULL (searched for such a check, a clamp, a default-reject arm, and a parameter-combination assertion in STEP 5; none exists). Demoted because the lenient policy combination is caller-selected with no producing or forbidding statement in this code, and the claimed impact (deployment of the unvalidated commit) happens only in the unshown caller.

commit_data receives no type validation in this code (no g_variant_is_of_type / g_variant_is_container check); the reachable consequences within this code are handled NULL paths, and no memory-unsafe access is performed by this code's own statements — all variant access goes through the GLib API.
required_metadata == NULL together with a present xa.metadata causes rejection via g_strcmp0 (NULL, xa) != 0 — fail-closed over-rejection with no security impact.

If a future caller invokes this function with require_xa_metadata == FALSE while relying on required_metadata being enforced, that caller would inherit a metadata-verification gap; this risk lives in the caller, not in the statements given here.

verdict.summary: In create_dump_dir_from_problem_data, items with CD_FLAG_BIN are processed (concat_path_file + copy_file) before — and therefore entirely bypassing — the only field-name validation (`if (name[0] == '.' || strchr(name, '/'))`), which sits after the branch's unconditional `continue`. An attacker-controlled problem_data hash key such as '../..'//...' escapes the dump directory, and copy_file writes attacker-chosen content (value->content as source) to an attacker-chosen destination with world-readable mode: arbitrary out-of-directory file write (path traversal).

evidence.reason: Sink and root cause: the attacker-controlled hash key `name` is used unchecked as the destination filename — `concat_path_file(dd->dd_dirname, name)` (line 78) builds the destination path and `copy_file(value->content, dest, DEFAULT_DUMP_DIR_MODE | S_IROTH)` (line 80) writes attacker-chosen content there. The only name validation in the function (line 91) is bypassed because this branch ends in `continue` (line 87), so BIN-item names containing '/' or '..' never reach it, despite the comment claiming 'only files should contain / and those are handled earlier'. Trigger fully instantiated: problem_data is attacker-data at this exported entry point; a BIN item named e.g. '../..//var/spool/pwned' with content '/tmp/payload' yields dest '/var/spool/abrt/<problem_id>/../..//var/spool/pwned' and an out-of-directory write with world-readable mode.

g_hash_table_iter_init(&iter, problem_data);
    while (g_hash_table_iter_next(&iter, (void**)&name, (void**)&value))
evidence.reason: Taint origin: `name` and `value->content`/`value->flags` are extracted directly from the caller-supplied `problem_data` hash table (parameter of this non-static exported function), which is attacker-data per the data-origin model; these unvalidated keys and paths flow into the path-assembly and copy sinks at lines 78 and 80.

assumptions: copy_file(value->content, dest, mode) copies file content from the source path value->content to the destination path dest — inferred from its name, the 'copying %s to %s' log, and the 'copied %li bytes' success message; its implementation is not shown.
concat_path_file joins its two path arguments with a '/' separator — standard semantics; its implementation is not shown.

Deployment/privilege context (e.g., whether this runs in a privileged daemon) is not evidenced in the given code and was not used to rank the finding; the out-of-directory write itself is the instantiated impact.
try_dd_create, dd_save_text, dd_rename, and problem_data_get_content_or_NULL implementations are not shown; their internal validation (or lack of it) could not be quoted.

The attacker-controlled `type` (FILENAME_ANALYZER content) is embedded in `problem_id` (line 38) and passed as a directory name to try_dd_create (lines 44/48/57/64) and dd_rename; traversal via a type containing '/' or '..' depends on validation inside not-shown callees, so no harm could be proven in this code.
uid_str validation (line 22: `INT_MAX < val`) permits negative longs; uid is only forwarded to try_dd_create/dd_create_basic_files, with no memory-unsafe or authz use visible in this code.

The log format at line 84 passes an `unsigned long` to '%li' — cosmetic only.

verdict.summary: smacker_read_header reads an attacker-controlled frame count from the media file (bounded only to 0xFFFFFF), performs unchecked av_malloc calls sized by that count (up to 64MB+16MB), and immediately dereferences the results in the frame-table read loops without any NULL check; the same unchecked-allocation pattern applies to av_new_stream in the audio loop. An attacker-supplied file with a large frames field induces allocation failure under attacker-scaled memory pressure, causing a NULL-pointer write at smk->frm_size[i] (or a NULL dereference at ast[i]->index) and crashing the process parsing the untrusted content — a denial-of-service. The code demonstrably knows the checking idiom (it checks !st for av_new_stream and !st->codec->extradata for av_malloc) but omits it for frm_size/frm_flags and the audio streams.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the av_malloc return values for frm_size and frm_flags are never checked (no NULL test exists on any path before first use, unlike the extradata check at line 85). Trigger: a crafted SMK file with frames = 0xFFFFFF passes the line-32 bound, forces av_malloc(67108860) and av_malloc(16777215); when either fails the loop at line 40 executes and line 41 writes through the NULL pointer, crashing the process on untrusted input.

evidence.snippet: smk->frames = get_le32(pb);
evidence.reason: Origin of the attacker-controlled value: the frame count is read directly from the untrusted media file and is the size selector for the unchecked allocations at lines 36-37 and the loop bound at lines 40/43; only an upper bound of 0xFFFFFF is enforced (line 32), which still permits ~80MB of attacker-demanded allocation per parsed file.

evidence.snippet:
ast[i] = av_new_stream(s, 0);
            smk->indexes[i] = ast[i]->index;
evidence.reason: Same unchecked-allocation defect: av_new_stream's return is dereferenced at line 70 with no NULL check (contrast the video stream's 'if (!st)' at lines 47-48). When the attacker-scaled allocations at lines 36-37 have consumed memory and the small AVStream allocation fails, ast[i]->index dereferences NULL.

assumptions: av_malloc and av_new_stream return NULL on failure (standard libc/FFmpeg allocation semantics; the code's own check 'if(!st->codec->extradata)' at line 85 confirms NULL is the failure sentinel of av_malloc in this codebase).

The declared types of SmackerContext fields (e.g., smk->frames, smk->treesize) are not shown; the comparisons at lines 20 and 32 only bound the values if those fields are unsigned/positive-width as their get_le32 assignments imply. If smk->frames were a signed int, a negative value (e.g., 0xFFFFFFFF) would bypass the 'frames > 0xFFFFFF' check, but that path still leads only to a failed huge av_malloc (NULL, loops skipped) inside this code, with any further use occurring in the not-shown read_packet.
get_le32/get_byte/get_buffer on a truncated file return short/zero data rather than aborting (assumed from typical ByteIOContext semantics; not shown).
limitations: pts_inc edge cases: pts_inc = 0 reaches av_reduce with den = 0, and pts_inc = INT32_MIN makes '-smk->pts_inc' (line 59) signed-overflow UB while 'smk->pts_inc *= 100' (line 61) overflows for pts_inc > 21474836; the arithmetic executes in this code, but every claimed consequence (division by zero, corrupted time_base) occurs inside av_reduce/av_set_pts_info, which are not shown, so the impact chain is not instantiated here.
width and height are unvalidated (up to 0xFFFFFFFF) but are only assigned to codec fields in this code; any out-of-bounds or misbehavior from them happens in the not-shown decoder.
frames = 0 yields av_malloc(0) results that this code never dereferences (loops skip); any harmful downstream use of frm_size/frm_flags lies in the not-shown read_packet.

The treesize check (line 20) allows allocations up to ~1GB (UINT_MAX/4) per parsed file from a tiny header, and that extradata is retained until context close — a bounded but large resource-consumption concern (CWE-400-like); the allocation itself is NULL-checked (line 85), so no corruption occurs in this code.

verdict.summary: dupstr allocates strlen(src)+1 bytes, checks the malloc result (exiting on failure), and copies exactly strlen+1 bytes including the terminator, so the measure/copy pair is self-consistent for all strings that can exist in memory. verdict.summary: pad_data computes *padded_len = data_len + padding with an unvalidated, attacker-controlled data_len (the only validation, 'if (!key || !data || key_len < 16)', omits data_len). For data_len near SIZE_MAX the sum wraps to a tiny value, malloc allocates that tiny buffer, and memcpy(padded_data, data, data_len)/memset then write ~SIZE_MAX attacker-length bytes out of bounds — a heap overflow in the exported encrypt_data API. Secondary: main ignores sscanf's return value, so non-hex argv content leaves key[i]/data[i] uninitialized heap bytes that are used as AES key material/plaintext and disclosed via the printed ciphertext and printed key.

evidence.reason: Root cause: unsigned integer overflow at '*padded_len = data_len + padding'. Instantiated trigger: a caller of the exported encrypt_data passes data_len = SIZE_MAX-15; padding = 16 - ((SIZE_MAX-15) % 16) = 16, so *padded_len wraps to 0, malloc(0) returns a minimal chunk, and memcpy writes SIZE_MAX-15 attacker bytes into it (memset then writes at a wild offset) — heap out-of-bounds write. No bound, clamp, or size check on data_len exists anywhere in this file.

evidence.snippet:
size_t padded_len;
    unsigned char* padded_data = pad_data(data, data_len, &padded_len);
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: the attacker-controlled data_len parameter of this exported function is passed unvalidated into pad_data; the only validation in the function, 'if (!key || !data || key_len < 16)', checks key_len but never data_len, so the overflow trigger in pad_data is reachable directly from the API's input surface.

Secondary confirmed defect: sscanf's return value is ignored, so for non-hex characters in argv[2] the conversion fails and data[i] keeps its uninitialized malloc'd heap value; that byte is encrypted and printed as ciphertext while the key used is also printed, disclosing uninitialized process heap memory (same pattern for key[i] at line 133). Trigger instantiated by running with a non-hex data argument.

assumptions: AES_BLOCK_SIZE is 16 (OpenSSL header, not shown in given code).

malloc(0) may return a non-NULL minimal allocation on the target allocator; if it returns NULL the candidate-1 failure path is taken without corruption, but standard allocators return non-NULL for size 0.
AES_set_encrypt_key with hardcoded 128 bits and a non-NULL key cannot fail (OpenSSL callee semantics, not shown in given code).

The only visible caller, main, derives data_len from strlen(argv[2])/2 and cannot itself produce a near-SIZE_MAX data_len; per the data-origin model the exported encrypt_data/pad_data parameters are nevertheless attacker-data, so the API surface is judged as the last line of defense.
limitations: Dangling pointers returned in 'result' on the error paths (lines 56-60, 63-67, 75-79, 83-88, 93-98 free result.iv/result.key and then return result) could cause a use-after-free read and double free in a caller that checks only encrypted_len — but with main as the shown caller the encrypted_data NULL check at line 144 short-circuits before any dereference, and the AES_set_encrypt_key failure arm is unreachable because the bit count is the hardcoded literal 128 and result.key is checked non-NULL; malloc/RAND failure paths require environment failures an attacker cannot induce. Speculative, not counted as a finding.

memcpy at line 14 also reads data_len bytes from the caller's 'data' pointer; a caller passing an inconsistent (data, data_len) pair causes an out-of-bounds read of the caller's buffer, but this code documents no data-length contract, so it is subsumed by the primary size-validation finding.
Padding is always in [1,16] (never zero) for all data_len, so no PKCS#7-style padding-collision defect exists here.

verdict.summary: get_ls_result returns the string literal "" on its error paths (pipe failure, fork failure, realloc failure) while its success paths return heap memory; the shown caller main unconditionally executes free(output) on the returned pointer, so any error path leads to free() of a non-heap static literal — undefined behavior, heap-metadata corruption/abort (CWE-590). The realloc-failure path is attacker-influenceable because the attacker-controlled dir_path drives an unbounded read-accumulate loop whose allocation can be forced to fail. Additionally, execlp("ls", ...) resolves the binary via the untrusted PATH environment with no absolute path or PATH sanitization anywhere in the code (CWE-426), allowing execution of an attacker-placed binary in the child.

evidence.reason: free(output) is executed on every return value of get_ls_result, but on the function's error paths that value is the string literal "" (lines 20, 25, 48), not heap memory. No check, ownership flag, or sentinel test exists between the call and the free, so any error path causes free() of a pointer into static read-only storage — invalid free / undefined behavior (CWE-590).

Origin of the faulty value: on realloc failure the function returns the non-heap literal "" while the caller frees the result. The realloc target size is driven by output_size, which accumulates the child's ls output in an unbounded loop; the attacker-controlled dir_path determines how much output ls produces, so the allocation failure (and thus the literal return feeding the invalid free in main) is attacker-influenceable. This path also leaks the previous buffer.

execlp resolves "ls" through the PATH environment variable; no statement in this code pins an absolute path (/bin/ls), sanitizes or sets PATH, or otherwise constrains the search element. An attacker-influenced PATH causes the child to execute an attacker-placed binary with the process's identity (CWE-426, untrusted search element).

assumptions: The only shown caller of get_ls_result is main (a CLI); privilege level and deployment context of the process are unknown and were not used to promote or demote any candidate.
The environment (PATH) consumed implicitly by execlp is inherited from the launching process; this code contains no statement that sets, clears, or validates it.
main's guard `if (argc != 2) { return 0; }` was treated as the documented non-NULL contract for argv[1] on the shown path; the CONTENT of dir_path is still attacker-data.
limitations: The pipe()-failure and fork()-failure triggers of the invalid free are pure environmental/OS failures that attacker data in the shown input surface cannot induce; the invalid free was instantiated instead via the realloc-failure path, where the attacker-controlled dir_path drives unbounded output accumulation until allocation fails. Even absent that, the free-of-literal is unconditional on every error path.

The read loop retains the child's entire ls output with no size cap (unbounded retention driven by attacker-chosen dir_path, CWE-400-adjacent); exploitation requires the attacker to pre-plant a very large directory in attacker-writable space, so it is recorded as a note rather than a separate primary finding.
realloc failure additionally loses the prior buffer pointer (memory leak); no security impact beyond resource loss was instantiated.

dir_path beginning with '-' can inject options into ls (e.g., --help, --sort) because it is passed as an operand without a `--` separator; only behavioral flag confusion, no quotable security impact in the shown code.

No shell is invoked (execlp with separate arguments), so classic shell metacharacter command injection (CWE-78 via `;`, `|`, backticks) is not available; the execution-sink defect is the PATH search element.

verdict.summary: The ssh_packet_kexdh_init callback is a state-gated dispatcher. The state check (session->dh_handshake_state != DH_STATE_INIT) is enforced on every path before dispatch; every switch arm including default assigns rc before its first read (default is fail-closed: ssh_set_error + rc = SSH_ERROR, followed by session_state = SSH_SESSION_STATE_ERROR); and unhandled kex types terminate the handshake fail-closed. The attacker-controlled packet body is consumed entirely inside the not-shown callees (ssh_server_kexdh_init/ecdh_init/curve25519_init), so no memory, index, injection, or authz sink exists in this code. The only unguarded aspects (possible NULL of session->next_crypto, possible unset kex_type before KEXINIT) cannot be instantiated from the given code and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: session->next_crypto is non-NULL when this callback runs; no allocation or NULL check is present in this code.
session->dh_handshake_state has a valid initial value and is only mutated by code not shown; its initial value (e.g., DH_STATE_INIT at session creation) is not shown.
The enum constant underlying an unset kex_type (value 0) is not defined in the given code; whether it maps to a handled case is unknown.
The callee handlers (ssh_server_kexdh_init, ssh_server_ecdh_init, ssh_server_curve25519_init) and their return-value ranges are not shown; only SSH_ERROR is distinguished here.
This callback's registration context (server-side only) is not shown; deployment context was not used to demote any candidate.

A client sending KEXDH_INIT before a completed KEXINIT negotiation would pass the dh_handshake_state check only if kex_type were left at an initial value that matches a handled case; both the initial state value and the enum's value-0 mapping are outside this code, so this trigger is speculative.

Unrecognized kex types (e.g., negotiated methods not enumerated in this switch) cause rc = SSH_ERROR and session_state = SSH_SESSION_STATE_ERROR, terminating that handshake; this is fail-closed and at most a single-connection degradation, not a security vulnerability.

Any occurrence of a single quote (or backslash) in 'text' terminates the intended string literal and injects attacker-chosen script into the page, yielding arbitrary JavaScript execution in the web page origin. No escaping or rejection of quote characters exists on any path in this function.

The desktop path (glfwSetClipboardString) shows no injection, copy, or interpreter sink in this code and was dismissed.

verdict.summary: decode_codestream uses s->curtileno as an index into the s->tile array at s->tile[s->curtileno] (and as the pointer offset s->tile + s->curtileno passed to init_tile/decode_packets) without any bounds check in this code. curtileno is the parse product of get_sot(s) over attacker-controlled codestream data (the SOT segment's tile index); no quotable statement documents or enforces a range for it, and the only guard, if (!(ret = get_sot(s))), tests only the callee's return status, not the index. An out-of-range tile index produces an out-of-bounds read in this function and hands attacker-derived pointers to subsequent decoding calls.

evidence.reason: Root cause: unvalidated index s->curtileno (set by the parse call get_sot(s) on attacker codestream data) is used to index s->tile with no bounds, clamp, assert, or error arm anywhere in the function (verified by exhaustive STEP 5 search). Trigger: attacker codestream with SOT marker and tile index (Isot) larger than the allocated tile count reaches line 43, causing an out-of-bounds read of struct fields at s->tile + curtileno*sizeof(J2kTile); the garbage pointers loaded become codsty/qntsty/properties for subsequent parsing.

Same unvalidated attacker-derived index s->curtileno computes an out-of-bounds tile pointer (s->tile + s->curtileno) on the SOD path, which is then passed as the tile argument to decode_packets; no range check on curtileno exists on any path in this code.

get_sot(s) is the producer of s->curtileno by parsing the SOT segment; its internal validation (if any) cannot be quoted from the given code, so curtileno is classified as attacker-data and the use in this code stands unguarded.
s->tile is allocated by get_siz (not shown); a small tile count (e.g. 1) versus a 16-bit attacker tile index is the instantiation used for the OOB read.
bytestream_get_be16 yields a non-negative 16-bit value (0..65535), so len-2 can be as low as -2 but the backward move stays inside the already-read buffer region.
limitations: s->buf += len - 2 (J2K_COM and default, lines 50 and 53) uses unvalidated len with no check that len-2 <= s->buf_end - s->buf, so s->buf can be pushed far past buf_end; however, every subsequent read in this function is preceded by the loop-top guard if (s->buf_end - s->buf < 2), which rejects the overshoot (negative difference) before any read, so no out-of-bounds read occurs in this code — the function merely logs 'Missing EOC' and returns 0. Not instantiated as a vulnerability here.

The consistency check if (s->buf - oldbuf != len || ret) (line 55) runs after the get_* callees have already consumed buffer bytes, so it cannot prevent over-consumption inside those not-shown callees.
get_qcc/get_qcd receive attacker-controlled len unvalidated; any harmful use of len occurs inside the not-shown callees.
A SOD marker before any SIZ/SOT lets s->tile + s->curtileno be computed from an unallocated/NULL s->tile; the dereference itself occurs in init_tile/decode_packets, which are not shown.

On error-free loop exit the function returns 0 even when the stream was truncated ('Missing EOC' path); presenting a decode-success state for a malformed stream has no instantiated security consequence in the given code.

verdict.summary: smtp_mailaddr validates its untrusted input on every path: line is NULL- and '<'-checked, the '>' write is in-bounds by strchr's guarantee and guarded by 'if (e == NULL) return (0);', the ':': strip uses memmove with strlen(p)+1 where p lies inside maddr->user, so the write range is a strict subset of the string's existing extent (a shrinking move that cannot overflow for any terminated input), and the domain default uses bounded strlcpy with sizeof(maddr->domain). The empty return-path acceptance is restricted to the RFC-mandated null sender by the conjunction of mailfrom, empty user, and empty domain, with all other addresses passing valid_localpart/valid_domainpart. All remaining risks depend on the not-shown callees (text_to_mailaddr's bounds/NUL-termination, struct mailaddr's field sizes) or on caller-pointer contracts that no attacker-controlled value can violate.

assumptions: struct mailaddr's user/domain fields are fixed-size arrays with at least 1 byte; their exact declaration is not given.

text_to_mailaddr (not shown) is assumed to write NUL-terminated, bounds-respecting values into maddr->user/maddr->domain; this code quotes no statement establishing NUL-termination, yet no statement in this code can produce a non-terminated user either.
valid_localpart and valid_domainpart (not shown) are assumed to perform the validation their names indicate.
domain and args are assumed non-NULL per an undocumented caller contract; no statement in this code documents or checks it.

The trigger state is producible only by a defect inside the callee; no statement or attacker input in this code instantiates it.

Speculative crash: *args = e and strlcpy(..., domain, ...) dereference caller-supplied pointers without NULL checks (CWE-476); args and domain are caller-created pointers, not attacker content, so no attacker-driven trigger exists in this code.

Semantic mangling, impact outside this code: a quoted local part containing ':' (e.g. <"a:b"@example.com>) is truncated at the first ':' by the memmove, rewriting the recipient; the mangled value still passes valid_localpart/valid_domainpart here, and any misdelivery consequence depends on delivery code not given. The ':' strip implements RFC 821 source-route (<@relay:user@final>) handling.
The in-place mutation *e++ = '\0' alters the caller's line buffer; harmless here since strchr located the position inside the string, but callers reusing line afterwards would observe truncation.

verdict.summary: In SProcXkbSelectEvents, the length guard `if (dataLeft < (size * 2))` is evaluated before the size==1 arm silently resets size to 2 in the trailing `else { size = 2; }`, after which `from.c8 += (size * 2); dataLeft -= (size * 2);` charge 4 bytes though only 2 were verified. With exactly 2 trailing bytes and one size-1 event bit set (e.g. XkbBellNotify), the unsigned counter dataLeft underflows to 0xFFFFFFFE and from.c8 moves 2 bytes past the request buffer; a subsequent size-2/size-4 event bit (e.g. XkbAccessXNotify) then passes the now-defeated guard and swaps()/swapl() read and write heap memory out of bounds. This is an attacker-triggerable heap OOB read/write (CVE-2015-0255 class) reachable by any X client.

evidence.reason: The bounds guard checks `dataLeft < (size * 2)` with size==1 (requiring only 2 bytes), but the else arm then resets size to 2 and lines 66-67 advance from.c8 and subtract 4. With dataLeft == 2 and a size-1 event bit (XkbBellNotify/XkbActionMessage/XkbCompatMapNotify), the unsigned dataLeft wraps to 0xFFFFFFFE and from.c8 passes the buffer end; the next size-2/size-4 event iteration passes the defeated guard and swaps()/swapl() perform out-of-bounds reads and writes of the heap-allocated request buffer. Trigger fully instantiated: affectWhich=(1<<8)|(1<<10), selectAll=clear=0, request length SIZEOF(xkbSelectEventsReq)+2.

Origin of the tainted values: from.c8 points into the client-controlled request buffer, dataLeft (declared `register unsigned` at line 20) holds the remaining attacker-controlled payload bytes, and the loop iterates over attacker-set affectWhich bits — the attacker chooses both the underflow condition (dataLeft == 2 with a size-1 event) and the subsequent size-2/4 event whose swaps then access memory out of bounds.

assumptions: REQUEST_AT_LEAST_SIZE(xkbSelectEventsReq) at line 6 is assumed (per its standard X-server macro semantics) to guarantee client->req_len*4 >= SIZEOF(xkbSelectEventsReq), so the initial dataLeft computation at line 23 does not itself underflow; the macro body is not shown in the given code.

The XKB event-bit constants (XkbBellNotify=8, XkbAccessXNotify=10, etc.) and the swaps/swapl macro semantics (in-place 2/4-byte read-modify-write) are taken from their standard definitions; the OOB conclusion does not depend on the exact bit values, only on the existence of both a size-1 and a size-2/4 case in the switch, which is quoted.

The request buffer is a heap allocation sized from the request length; the underflow simulation uses a request of SIZEOF(xkbSelectEventsReq)+2 bytes, which the length-swapped stuff->length at line 5 lets the client specify.
limitations: The size==1 arm also fails to byte-swap the per-event detail bytes it consumes (functional defect with no direct memory-safety impact); it is subsumed by the primary underflow finding.

A single size==1 event bit with dataLeft==2 only advances the pointer past the buffer without dereferencing; the OOB access requires at least one further size-2 or size-4 event bit in affectWhich, which is fully attacker-selectable.

verdict.summary: In r_bin_java_rti_annotations_attr_new, the annotation-parsing loop validates the buffer-relative offset against the total buffer size ('offset >= sz') and passes 'sz - offset' as the remaining size to r_bin_java_annotation_new, omitting subtraction of buf_offset. Since the entry guard 'buf_offset + 32 >= sz' establishes that sz is the total buffer size while buffer points at absolute offset buf_offset, any attribute placed at buf_offset > 0 in an attacker-crafted class file causes the callee to be granted up to buf_offset bytes beyond the real data, and the loop keeps invoking it with buffer + offset past the end of the buffer (offset is only advanced by the unvalidated, attacker-derived annotation->size). The result is a heap out-of-bounds read while parsing attacker-supplied Java class-file annotation content.

evidence.reason: The loop guard compares the buffer-LOCAL offset against the TOTAL size sz, so it fails to break at the true data boundary offset == sz - buf_offset whenever buf_offset > 0 (edge case: at offset == sz - buf_offset the check 'offset >= sz' is false and the loop continues). The callee is then passed 'sz - offset' as its size, which overstates the bytes actually available at buffer + offset by exactly buf_offset. With buf_offset = 160, sz = 200, offset = 8: the callee is told 192 bytes remain when only 32 do; after offset += annotation->size (line 20, unvalidated) reaches 108, the next iteration calls r_bin_java_annotation_new with a pointer 68 bytes past the end of the buffer and a claimed size of 92 — an out-of-bounds read of attacker-chosen extent while parsing annotation content.

This guard is the only in-code statement fixing the coordinate space of sz: it demands more than 32 bytes at the ABSOLUTE offset buf_offset, which is coherent only if sz is the total buffer size and buffer points at absolute offset buf_offset. It also proves that 'offset' (buffer-relative, per 'offset += 6' and 'R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT (buffer, offset)') and sz are in different coordinate spaces, so the loop's 'offset >= sz' and 'sz - offset' computations at lines 15 and 18 are unit-confused. This entry guard covers only the first 33 bytes and never re-applies inside the loop.

assumptions: sz is the total class-file buffer size and buffer points at absolute offset buf_offset within it; this is inferred from the dimensional form of the guard 'buf_offset + 32 >= sz' (the caller is not shown, but under the alternative reading the guard is dimensionally meaningless and would reject every attribute past the file midpoint).

r_bin_java_annotation_new treats its second parameter as the number of bytes readable from its first parameter; the callee body is not given, but the false bound 'sz - offset' is computed and passed by this code.

attr->info.rtv_annotations_attr.num_annotations and attr->info.annotation_array.num_annotations are assumed to be same-layout union members (struct {ut16; RList*}); the union definition is not shown. If the layouts differ, the loop bound would additionally be an uninitialized read (CWE-908).
R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT(buffer, offset) reads a 2-byte big-endian value at buffer[offset]; macro body not shown.
limitations: Unsigned wraparound of 'buf_offset + 32' (requires buf_offset >= 2^64-32) would bypass the entry guard and allow the read at offset 6 with fewer than 8 bytes; no statement in this code can produce such a buf_offset, so this trigger is speculative.

The actual out-of-bounds dereference is performed inside r_bin_java_annotation_new (not given); the defect attributed to this code is computing and passing the false remaining size 'sz - offset' and guarding the offset with the wrong quantity sz.
annotation->size == 0 causes up to num_annotations (max 65535) non-advancing iterations reparsing the same bytes — bounded amplification, minor.

The r_list_newf return value is not NULL-checked before r_list_append, and a NULL annotation is appended when parsing fails — allocation-failure/robustness issues with no attacker-triggerable security effect in this code.

verdict.summary: In this rlm_unix password-lookup module, the attacker-controlled User-Name is used only as a lookup key and log argument (%s), all lookup failures are checked with early NOTFOUND/REJECT returns, and no statement in the given code can itself produce the NULL field values, out-of-range sizes, or injected content that the remaining candidates would require. The NULL-dereference of encrypted_pass (possible NULL sp_pwdp/pw_passwd), the passwordless-account NOOP path, the shadow-expiry bypass when the passwd password is >= 10 chars, and a potential pairmove/pairfree lifetime issue all fail trigger or impact instantiation within this code: their triggering values come from not-shown NSS backends, and their security consequences (accept/reject decisions, list ownership) occur in not-shown callers/callees. No guard I could require was found missing on any path whose trigger is realizable from this code's own input surface.

assumptions: request->username->vp_strvalue is assumed to be a NUL-terminated string buffer maintained by the (not shown) RADIUS request parser; the code's only own guarantee is the quoted 'if (!request->username) return RLM_MODULE_NOOP;' on the pair pointer, not on the string contents.

The semantics of getpwnam/getspnam/getprpwnam field population (whether pw_passwd, sp_pwdp, pw_shell, fd_encrypt can be NULL for a successful lookup) are determined by not-shown platform/NSS implementations; no statement in this code documents or asserts them.
The meaning of the RLM_MODULE_NOOP return value to the caller (authorize/authentication pipeline) is not shown; this code only returns it, it does not itself accept or reject authentication.
pairmove/pairmake/pairfree semantics (whether pairmove consumes *vp) are not shown; the in-code comment '/* might not be NULL; */' indicates pairfree is expected to tolerate either state.
Which preprocessor flags (OSFC2, HAVE_GETSPNAM, HAVE_GETUSERSHELL, DENY_SHELL, __FreeBSD__, _PWF_EXPIRE) are set is a build-time condition not derivable from the code.
limitations: NULL dereference candidate at 'if (encrypted_pass[0] == 0)': the code checks 'if ((encrypted_pass == NULL) || (strlen(encrypted_pass) < 10))' before consulting shadow but performs NO NULL check after 'encrypted_pass = spwd->sp_pwdp;' (and none at all on the pwd->pw_passwd assignment when HAVE_GETSPNAM is undefined). A NULL check at the sink is genuinely absent (verified by exhaustive search in STEP 5). However, the triggering value (sp_pwdp/pwd->pw_passwd == NULL) is produced only by not-shown NSS backends and cannot be instantiated from this code's own inputs or statements, so the candidate is speculative per STEP 4(a).

Fail-open candidate: a passwordless account reaches 'if (encrypted_pass[0] == 0) return RLM_MODULE_NOOP;' — the module declines to act (and its FIXME comment acknowledges the ambiguity) instead of rejecting. The trigger is fully instantiated (attacker supplies the username of a passwordless account), but the security consequence (acceptance) depends entirely on how the not-shown caller treats RLM_MODULE_NOOP; the impact chain breaks at an unquoted link.

Expiration-bypass candidate: when 'strlen(encrypted_pass) >= 10' the shadow lookup is skipped, spwd stays NULL, and 'if (spwd && spwd->sp_expire > 0 && ...)' silently skips the expiry check. Exploitation requires a specific system configuration (>= 10-char password field in passwd coexisting with an expiring shadow entry) that neither the attacker's input nor any statement in this code produces.
strcmp(pwd->pw_shell, DENY_SHELL) with a hypothetically NULL pw_shell would crash, but pw_shell NULL-ness is again callee-determined and not instantiable from this code.
A potential double-free/ownership issue between 'pairmove(vp_list, &vp);' and 'pairfree(&vp);' depends on pairmove's (not shown) consumption semantics and cannot be proven from the given code.

verdict.summary: ff_h264_pred_weight_table uses the attacker-controlled, unvalidated parameter ref_count[list] as loop bound (line 27) and then writes pwt->luma_weight[16 + 2*i] and [16 + 2*i + 1] (and chroma equivalents) in the PICT_FRAME path. No check in this code bounds ref_count or the derived index. With a bitstream specifying frame pictures and ref_count > 8, i reaches 8 and index 16+2*i = 32 exceeds the 32-entry first dimension of H264PredWeightTable.luma_weight, producing an out-of-bounds write with attacker-influenced value and attacker-controlled offset; larger ref_count (up to the spec-legal 32) drives writes to index 78 and also makes the direct [i] stores out of bounds for ref_count > 32.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The index 16 + 2*i (+1) must satisfy 16 + 2*i + 1 <= 31 (i.e. i <= 7 for the [32]-entry arrays of H264PredWeightTable), but i is bounded only by the unvalidated attacker-controlled ref_count[list] from line 27. Trigger instantiated: a slice header with picture_structure == PICT_FRAME and ref_count[list] = 16 makes i = 8 write pwt->luma_weight[32][list][0], one past the 32-entry first dimension, with the attacker-influenced value luma_def (1<<denom, 1..128), a parsed weight ([-128,127]), or 0; ref_count = 32 drives writes up to index 78 and corrupts adjacent struct members.

evidence.snippet: for (i = 0; i < ref_count[list]; i++) {
evidence.reason: Origin of the faulty bound: ref_count is a content-carrying parameter of this non-static exported parser (values parsed by the caller from PPS/slice headers, attacker-controlled up to 32 per the H.264 grammar) and is never checked, clamped, or compared against any limit anywhere in this function; the loop condition is the sole bound for the index used at the sinks on lines 31-32, 42-43, 50-51, 64-65 and 71-76, so any ref_count above the array capacity flows directly into out-of-bounds writes.

assumptions: The type H264PredWeightTable is not part of the given code; its members luma_weight/chroma_weight are assumed to have 32-entry first dimensions ([32][2][2] and [32][2][2][2]) as in FFmpeg's h264_parse.h. Even under any larger plausible dimension, the 16-offset duplication design implies valid duplication indices are [16,31], and the spec-legal maximum ref_count of 32 drives indices up to 78, still out of bounds.
pwt and logctx are assumed non-NULL at the interface level; no dereference-only path in this code can be shown to fail on NULL beyond ordinary member writes/logging.

The caller is assumed to pass values derived from the H.264 bitstream for ref_count, slice_type_nos, and picture_structure (frame pictures, PICT_FRAME, are the common attacker-selectable case); no caller-side bound on ref_count is quoted because none exists in the given code, and per guard anchoring such an unquoted check cannot be relied on.
sps->chroma_format_idc is assumed to be a parsed value in [0,3]; it only selects code paths here and does not bound indices.
limitations: If ref_count[list] never exceeded 8 (frame) / 32 (any) in a given deployment, the trigger would not fire; however, the H.264 grammar permits num_ref_idx up to 32, so no evidence in the given code bounds it — this is recorded only to note that the frame-mode duplication at i<=7 is in bounds.

The out-of-bounds writes for 8 <= i <= 15 land within the surrounding H264PredWeightTable struct (corrupting chroma_weight and later members); exploitation primitives beyond struct corruption depend on the struct's embedding in the heap-allocated decoder context, which is not shown.

verdict.summary: display_dollar() clamps its column parameter only against negative values ('colnr_T col = col_arg < 0 ? 0 : col_arg;') and never checks it against the length of the current line. It then constructs the pointer 'p + col' from ml_get_curline() and passes it to mb_head_off() ('curwin->w_cursor.col -= (*mb_head_off)(p, p + col);'). When col exceeds the byte length of the line (e.g., col = 100 for a 2-byte line), p + col points past the end of the heap buffer, and mb_head_off reads memory at/around that address, causing a heap out-of-bounds read. col_arg is a parameter of an exported, non-static handler whose value derives from untrusted edited-file content and cursor/virtual-column state, and no statement in this code bounds it above; the sole guard ('col_arg < 0') rejects only negative values and lets every col > line length through.

evidence.snippet:
p = ml_get_curline();
	curwin->w_cursor.col -= (*mb_head_off)(p, p + col);
evidence.reason: Sink: 'p + col' is formed from the current line pointer and the unvalidated column 'col' and passed to mb_head_off, which dereferences that address. With col = 100 and the current line being 2 bytes plus NUL, p + col points 98 bytes past the end of the heap allocation, producing an out-of-bounds read. The only comparison on col anywhere in the function is the lower-bound clamp on line 3; no upper bound against STRLEN(p) or any line length exists on any path to line 18, and curs_columns() on line 20 runs after the use and cannot protect it.

evidence.snippet: colnr_T col = col_arg < 0 ? 0 : col_arg;
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: the sole validation of the exported function's parameter clamps only the negative range; it provides no upper bound, so any col_arg greater than the current line's byte length reaches the pointer arithmetic 'p + col' on line 18 unchanged. Edge case col_arg = STRLEN(p)+1 (one past the NUL terminator) is accepted by this clamp.

assumptions: colnr_T is a signed integer column type and ml_get_curline() returns a NUL-terminated heap buffer holding the current line whose content and length come from the edited (untrusted) file; neither the typedef nor the callee is shown in the given code.

has_mbyte, redrawing(), and the cursor/window globals are editor state that the surrounding (not shown) editor mutates in response to the edited content; no statement in this code constrains them, so they are treated as attacker-influenced state per the data-origin model.

mb_head_off(p, q) inspects bytes at and before q, as its documented purpose ('move to the first byte') and the subtraction of its result imply; the dereference itself occurs in the helper, but the out-of-bounds pointer p + col is computed and passed by this code.
limitations: Candidate C2: storing an unbounded col into curwin->w_cursor.col (line 11) before curs_columns(FALSE) (line 20) could propagate an out-of-range column into the callee, but curs_columns is not shown and no harmful use of that value is instantiated within this code, so its impact chain is unquoted.

Candidate C3: a potential underflow of 'curwin->w_cursor.col -= (*mb_head_off)(...)' was not instantiated for in-bounds inputs, since mb_head_off's return is an offset within the string and cannot exceed col when p + col is in bounds; when p + col is out of bounds the behavior is already covered by the primary out-of-bounds-read finding.

The precise disclosure capability of the out-of-bounds read depends on mb_head_off's implementation (not shown); the confirmed defect is the out-of-bounds pointer construction and consumption of unvalidated attacker-derived column data at line 18.

verdict.summary: In SKIP_TYPE_ROW and SKIP_TYPE_COL, only the single row/column flag bit is checked with get_bits_left(); the inner 'else' loops then call get_bits1() once per macroblock (up to mb_width or mb_height times) with no bits-left check, so an attacker-crafted bitstream drives the bit reader arbitrarily far past the end of the input buffer (an out-of-bounds read of attacker-scalable depth whose result also feeds the mb_type flags), and the function still returns 0 (success).

evidence.reason: SKIP_TYPE_ROW else branch: the guard 'if (get_bits_left(&s->gb) < 1) return AVERROR_INVALIDDATA;' (lines 24-25) covers only the row-flag bit, yet this loop consumes one bit per macroblock (mb_width bits) via get_bits1 with no bits-left check on any path inside the loop. Trigger instantiated: bits_left==1 passes the check, the flag bit (attacker set to 0) consumes it, then the loop reads with bits_left = 0, -1, -2, ... up to mb_width times per row — an out-of-bounds read of the bitstream buffer of attacker-controlled depth, while the function returns 0.

SKIP_TYPE_COL else branch: identical defect; the check 'if (get_bits_left(&s->gb) < 1) return AVERROR_INVALIDDATA;' (lines 39-40) covers only the column-flag bit while this loop performs mb_height unchecked get_bits1 calls, driving the reader past the buffer end by an attacker-chosen amount via stream-controlled mb_height.

assumptions: s->gb is a bitstream reader over attacker-controlled compressed frame data (this function parses frame content: skip_type, per-MB skip flags), which is the basis for treating the bitstream as untrusted; no statement in this code initializes or constrains s->gb.

s->mb_width, s->mb_height, and s->mb_stride are set outside this function from stream-derived picture dimensions; no statement in this code asserts mb_stride >= mb_width or any bound on the dimensions.
The allocation size of s->current_picture_ptr->mb_type is not established by any statement in this code.

get_bits1/get_bits/get_bits_left semantics (index arithmetic over the buffer) are external; the out-of-bounds memory access itself occurs inside the not-shown reader, but this function is the intake point that decides how many bits to consume and omits the very check it uses elsewhere (lines 15, 24-25, 39-40).
limitations: Candidate: OOB write to mb_type if mb_stride < mb_width or the array is undersized — speculative; no statement in this code produces such a state, and no allocation or stride-setting code is shown.

Candidate: integer overflow of 's->mb_height * s->mb_width' in the line 15 guard — requires dimensions whose product exceeds INT_MAX; no statement in this code can produce such dimensions, so the trigger is speculative.
Candidate: missing default arm for the 2-bit skip_type — four SKIP_TYPE_* cases are shown covering the 2-bit range; no out-of-range value is instantiable from this code.

The precise overread distance that escapes any buffer padding maintained by the (not shown) bitstream allocation cannot be bounded from this code; the code shown bounds overread only by mb_width*mb_height bits, which is attacker-scalable but finite.

verdict.summary: This calloc wrapper correctly guards the size computation n*lb against size_t overflow with the canonical check 'if (lb && n > SIZE_MAX / lb) return NULL;', which executes first in order, covers both multiplication uses (GC_malloc_uncollectable and REDIRECT_MALLOC), short-circuits the division by zero case for lb==0, and uses the correct boundary operator (allowing n == SIZE_MAX/lb exactly, whose product cannot exceed SIZE_MAX). No unguarded memory, index, injection, crypto, or authz sink exists in this code.

assumptions: REDIRECT_MALLOC is a malloc-family allocator whose behavior for size 0 and for sizes near SIZE_MAX (returning NULL on failure) is not shown; standard malloc semantics are assumed, not quoted.
GC_malloc_uncollectable's internal handling of the pre-validated n*lb value is not shown; no harmful use of that value occurs within this code.
GC_init_lib_bounds correctly setting GC_libpthread_start/_end and GC_libld_start/_end is not shown; these are internal-trusted globals, not attacker data.
limitations: Candidate 'integer overflow in n*lb reaching allocation sizing (CWE-190)' was tested and rejected: the quoted guard 'if (lb && n > SIZE_MAX / lb)' at the top of the function precedes both uses of n*lb in execution order and rejects every overflowing boundary pair (e.g., n=SIZE_MAX, lb=2).

Candidate 'unchecked REDIRECT_MALLOC result' rejected: returning NULL on allocation failure is the malloc-family interface's defined error signal; no corruption, bypass, or misrepresentation occurs in this code.
Candidate 'division by zero in SIZE_MAX / lb' rejected: the short-circuit 'lb &&' in the guard prevents it when lb==0.

verdict.summary: Fail-open input validation in smtp_mailaddr: when the combined check at lines 29-30 fails, the 'no domain, local user' branch (lines 40-43) returns 1 (accepted) after only testing maddr->user for emptiness, never re-running valid_localpart(maddr->user). An attacker-supplied unqualified address such as RCPT TO:<bad|user> whose local part failed the charset/length validator reaches 'return (1)' at line 43, so the mail-address validation gate presents the accepted state for an address that failed verification.

The user-supplied regex pattern is fully sanitized before compilation: escapeRegex escapes every ECMAScript metacharacter ('^ $ . * + ? ( ) [ ] { } | \') on every iteration before the character is appended, so no attacker-constructible quantifier, alternation, class, or anchor can reach std::regex_search — the ReDoS sink is guarded. Compilation/matching errors fail closed via the catch(regex_error) -> return false path, matching the documented contract. The only genuine defect is that main dereferences argv[1]/argv[2] without checking argc, a NULL-pointer UB crash; its trigger (argc<3) is an invocation-shape property that no content-carrying party across a trust boundary can instantiate, and no shared/higher-privileged deployment is evidenced in the code, so it is recorded as a limitation, not a vulnerability.

assumptions: The deployment of main() (local CLI, setuid binary, or wrapper-spawned backend) is not evidenced by the given code; per discipline 3 it was not used to promote or demote any candidate.
std::regex uses the default ECMAScript grammar (no std::regex::flag argument at line 27 changes the metacharacter set).
argv[1]/argv[2] are non-NULL whenever argc>=3, per the C runtime contract; the code itself contains no argc check to quote.
limitations: C2 (missing argc check, lines 36-37: 'std::string pattern = argv[1];' / 'std::string content = argv[2];'): invoking the program with fewer than 3 arguments passes NULL to a std::string constructor — undefined behavior, typically a segfault (CWE-476). Confirmed absent-guard in STEP 5 (no bounds/NULL check exists anywhere in main), but the trigger requires the invoking party to omit arguments; the party that controls pattern/content values (per the in-code docstring, remote users of the 'pattern search Web API') cannot cause argc<3 through any content value, and no shared or higher-privileged execution context is evidenced, so the crash is not an instantiated cross-trust-boundary DoS. Robustness bug, not scored.

C3: std::bad_alloc from compiling a huge escaped pattern or from escapeRegex's growth (at most 2x input) is not caught by the regex_error handler and would terminate the process; trigger requires memory exhaustion at ~1:1 input scale — environment failure, not attacker-scalable amplification.

C4: an empty pattern compiles to an empty regex, which matches at position 0 and prints 'true'; this is consistent with the documented semantics ('True if the pattern is found') and carries no security-state meaning.

Literal-pattern std::regex_search cost is worst-case proportional to pattern-length x content-length in typical implementations; both operands are attacker-supplied in principle, but no request-size bound or wrapper behavior is shown, so no concrete amplification factor can be instantiated from the given code.

verdict.summary: qemu_register_machine performs no parsing, arithmetic, indexing, or copying of attacker content; its only risky uses are the unvalidated pointer parameters m and m->name passed to g_strconcat, whose NULL-dereference trigger depends entirely on caller-supplied state that no statement in this code instantiates. No guard exists in the code (verified), but no trigger or security impact chain can be simulated from this code's own input surface, so no in-code vulnerability is confirmed.

assumptions: type_register(&ti) is assumed to validate or abort on bad input and to duplicate or take ownership of ti.name; its behavior is not shown in the given code and cannot be quoted.
g_strconcat is assumed to be GLib's g_strconcat, which requires a non-NULL first string; its internal strlen/guard behavior is callee code not shown.

The intended deployment (registration of a static machine table at init time) is context assumed from the QEMU codebase, not quotable from the given code; per discipline 3 it was not used to dismiss candidates.
limitations: Candidate C1/C2 (NULL or non-terminated m / m->name dereferenced at the g_strconcat(m->name, ...) expression, line 4, CWE-476): no guard exists anywhere in this code (STEP 5 search confirmed: no NULL check, assert, g_return_val_if_fail, or failure-sentinel test on any path), but the trigger requires the not-shown caller to pass NULL or a bad m->name; no statement in this code parses or produces that value, and the worst direct consequence is process termination, so the trigger is speculative under STEP 4 and the candidate is not counted as a vulnerability in this code.

Candidate C3: g_strconcat at line 4 may return NULL on allocation failure; the result is stored in ti.name and passed to type_register at line 9 unchecked, but the trigger requires environment/OOM failure no attacker can induce and the impact link lies inside the not-shown type_register callee.

Candidate C4: the heap string allocated by g_strconcat (line 4) is never freed in this code; at worst a fixed-size registration-time leak with no attacker-scalable retention, contingent on unshown type_register ownership semantics.

verdict.summary: No attacker-instantiated vulnerability found. The unchecked V8 casts are guarded in correct execution order by '!descriptor->IsObject()' and '!getter->IsFunction()', the Maybe-empty failure sentinels are tested before first use, and 'result' is returned only on the success path of '.ToLocal(&result)'. The remaining candidates (NULL className/attributeName reaching fprintf %s, RELEASE_NOTREACHED crash on lookup miss, attacker-controlled descriptor 'get' dispatch, TryCatch installed after initializeHolderIfNeeded) each require a precondition that no statement in this code instantiates: they originate in callers or callees not shown and are recorded as assumptions/limitations.

assumptions: No statement in this code documents, asserts, or checks non-NULL for className or attributeName; the belief that callers (generated Blink bindings) always pass valid literals is an unquoted interface contract, not evidence.

classObjectOfPrivateScript, v8String, initializeHolderIfNeeded, rethrowExceptionInPrivateScript, and V8ScriptRunner::callFunction are callees not shown; their internal safety, their exception behavior, and the isolation of the private-script context from web content cannot be verified from the given code.

Deployment context (renderer-internal helper not reachable directly from web content) was not used as evidence; the demotion of the RELEASE_NOTREACHED crash rests on the un-instantiatable attacker trigger, not on assumed deployment.
limitations: fprintf(stderr, ..., className, attributeName) with a NULL or unterminated name pointer would be UB/crash (and RELEASE_NOTREACHED terminates the process on any lookup miss), but no statement in this code produces or permits such an input; trigger is speculative.

If a lower-privileged party could mutate the private-script class object or plant a Proxy so that GetOwnPropertyDescriptor returns an attacker-chosen 'get' function, the V8ScriptRunner::callFunction dispatch would execute attacker code; the corrupting write exists only in a callee not shown and no attacker-derived value is passed to classObjectOfPrivateScript here.
initializeHolderIfNeeded executes before the v8::TryCatch is installed; if that callee can throw, the exception path is unhandled in this function, but the callee's behavior is not shown.

RELEASE_NOTREACHED on the two error paths is a deliberate fail-fast; treating it as a DoS would require an attacker-reachable entry with arbitrary className/attributeName, which is not demonstrable from this code.

verdict.summary: html_escape and get_welcome_message correctly size, escape, and null-check their data. The two-pass count/write loops in html_escape use identical per-character increments and identical entity strings, so the malloc(len+1) buffer is always exactly sufficient (verified with empty input and all-'&' boundary inputs). get_welcome_message computes total_length as strlen(prefix)+strlen(escaped)+strlen(suffix)+1, which exactly matches the bytes written by strcpy/strcat/strcat. All allocation and NULL failure sentinels are tested before first use, and all five HTML-significant characters are escaped before the value is embedded in a page-rendered message. Only theoretical size_t-overflow triggers at ~SIZE_MAX/6 input scales and an uninstantiable TOCTOU between the two passes exist; neither is reachable from this code's input surface.

assumptions: Execution is single-threaded with respect to the input buffer; nothing in the given code spawns threads or exposes the buffer for concurrent mutation, so the two-pass traversal of input is assumed consistent.
size_t is at least 32 bits; the code declares size_t and lets the platform define its width.
limitations: Theoretical: len (size_t) in html_escape's counting loop can wrap only with an input of roughly SIZE_MAX/6 bytes (≈3 exabytes on 64-bit), which the counting loop itself must fully traverse; the trigger cannot be instantiated from this code's input surface, and no guard against it exists.
Theoretical: total_length = strlen(prefix)+strlen(escaped_username)+strlen(suffix)+1 can wrap only if the escaped allocation approaches SIZE_MAX bytes; speculative for the same reason.

Theoretical TOCTOU: if the input string were concurrently modified between html_escape's counting pass and writing pass, the write could overflow the buffer; no two ordered operations with an attacker interleaving window exist in this code.
strcpy/strcat (CWE-676-class functions) are used, but with a correctly computed buffer size (exact byte accounting verified), so no overflow exists as written.
